note:
God calls Jeremiah to his prophetic ministry of announcing divine judgment on Judah for idolatry. OT prophets were called and appointed by God, following the pattern of the archetypal prophet, Moses (see Deut. 18:15; Ex. 3).

**1:1–3** Jeremiah prophesied over a forty-year period during the reign of several kings up to the Babylonian exile of the people of Judah. During this time, the word of the Lord came to him repeatedly (25:3). His prophecies are not recorded in chronological order in his book, however.

**1:1 priests who were in Anathoth.** Anathoth was a priestly city from early times (Josh. 21:17, 18); cf. 11:21–23. Jeremiah was both a prophet and a priest, like Ezekiel and Zechariah.

verse_quote: to whom the word of the LORD came.
note:
This phrase often opens prophetic books (cf. Hos. 1:1; Joel 1:1; Mic. 1:1). Jeremiah’s recorded words, therefore, are God’s words (1 Pet. 1:10–12; 2 Pet. 1:21), though they also reflect the style and experiences of the human author.

**Josiah.** A godly king who undertook a major religious reform beginning in 628 B.C. (2 Kin. 22; 23; 2 Chr. 34; 35); Jeremiah approved of him (22:11, 15, 16), though he makes few specific references to the reform.

**thirteenth year.** 626 B.C.

Josiah’s son, who reversed many of his father’s reforms after Josiah’s death in 609 B.C., reigned for eleven years (2 Kin. 23:36–24:7). He was briefly preceded as king by his brother Jehoahaz, who reigned for three months before being exiled to Egypt.

**Zedekiah.** Jehoiakim’s younger brother, who succeeded him after the three-month reign of Jehoiachin (2 Kin. 24:8–15), whom Nebuchadnezzar took to Babylon in 597 B.C. All four of the kings of Judah after Josiah did evil in the Lord’s sight, seeking to use human wisdom in the face of considerable political and military pressure from Egypt and Babylon. Yet the outcome of these policies was the almost-complete destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, just as Jeremiah prophesied.

God’s creation and election of Jeremiah belong together (for the verb “know” in the sense of “choose,” see Gen. 18:19; Amos 3:2). This setting apart before birth is the ground of Jeremiah’s prophetic standing. Compare also Moses, whose birth narrative (Ex. 2) has the same meaning, and Paul (Gal. 1:15). It is not possible to refuse God’s sovereign commissioning.

**to the nations.** Jeremiah’s message is chiefly for Judah, but he has words of judgment for other nations as well (25:8–37; 46–51). These oracles of judgment against the nations are designed to encourage God’s people that the covenant with Abraham in Gen. 12:1–3 is still intact, for this covenant promises judgment on those who harmed Israel.

verse_quote: I do not know how to speak.
note:
Moses made a similar protest (Ex. 4:10).

**youth.** Denotes a disqualifying immaturity (1 Kin. 3:7). It is common for prophets to object that they are unqualified for the task (cf. Is. 6:5).

The reassurance necessarily recurs (10:5; 30:10; cf. Is. 43:1; Luke 12:32). The Lord who has formed and called him is able to judge whether he was capable of the task.

**I am with you.** These words are the Lord’s essential promise to His people (Ex. 3:12; Is. 7:14; Matt. 1:23; 28:20).

Indicates that Jeremiah is consecrated to speak the Lord’s words (Is. 6:7).

**words in your mouth.** See Ex. 4:15; 2 Pet. 1:21.

The images emphasize Jeremiah’s message of destruction, while also foreshadowing the Lord’s reconstruction. The narrative of his call prepares for the prophet’s ministry in all its variety. If the people will not repent, their destruction is sure. Yet God nonetheless has good plans for the remnant of His people (29:11). God’s word always accomplishes God’s purposes (Is. 55:11).

The term can also designate revelatory visions (Amos 7:8). The first of these visions shows a branch of an almond tree. There is a play on words here: the Hebrew word for “almond” (_shaqed_) sounds like the word for “watching” (_shoqed_). Since almond trees are among the first trees to blossom in the spring, they represent the change of the seasons.

The second vision is a boiling pot about to tip over from the north. Though Babylon lies to the east of Judah, the Babylonians’ route of march will bring them to Judah from the north, as with many of Judah’s historical enemies., 14

Judgment is a work of God (11:2) wherein He implements the curses of the covenant in relation to His covenant people (Deut. 28:15–68).

**forsaking me ... other gods.** Judah’s basic sin is apostasy; they have forsaken the Lord and bowed down to idols, provoking His wrath. The central issue in the book is faithfulness to God.

**made offerings.** See note on 11:13.

**works of their own hands.** This is an ironic polemic (Is. 46:6).
Lit. “gird up your loins” (text note). Refers to tucking the long flowing robe that people wore into a belt in preparation for battle or other activities (1 Kin. 18:46; 1 Pet. 1:13).

verse_quote: fortified city ... iron pillar ... bronze walls.
note:
The Lord will enable Jeremiah to stand firm in the face of fierce opposition.

**kings ... land.** Jeremiah’s accusation will embrace the whole society of Judah, from greatest to least.

Jeremiah uses a number of vivid images (such as comparing Judah to a wild donkey and a prostitute) to indict Judah for unfaithfulness to God (2:1–3:5) and to warn of certain judgment if the nation will not repent and return to God (3:6–6:30).

In Hebrew, cities are personified as feminine (7:29 note).

**devotion.** On the Hebrew _hesed_, see note on Ps. 36:5.

**youth ... bride.** Israel’s early relationship with the Lord in the wilderness after the exodus from Egypt is remembered as pure and devoted, like a bride’s with her groom. See Hos. 2:14–16 for a similar image. The prophets often use the reverse image of adultery to describe the idolatry of God’s people.

These terms are drawn from the life of worship. As a holy nation, Israel has been dedicated to the Lord (Ezek. 22:26); a “firstfruit” is the first part of the harvest that belongs specifically to the Lord (Deut. 26:2; Hos. 9:10).

**incurred guilt.** The offense results from unauthorized handling of holy things.

verse_quote: I brought you into a plentiful land.
note:
Israel (specifically Judah, as the northern kingdom is in exile when Jeremiah is ministering) has forgotten the One that had been so good to her in bringing her into the land and caring for her. In vv. 8, 9, three groups of leaders will be indicted for the offense.

**defiled my land ... my heritage.** See Deut. 21:23. God’s holy people (Deut. 7:6) dwell in the land He gave them for a heritage, a plentiful and fertile land. The land can be defiled, or in religious terms be made “unclean” by sin, because it remains God’s possession. See Lev. 25:23.

These may also be “those who handle the law” (cf. 18:18; Deut. 31:9), or the latter may be a scribal group (8:8).

**shepherds.** A figure often used for rulers (23:1–4). The Lord promises that He will give unfaithful Israel faithful shepherds in the future.

**prophets.** An official group that Jeremiah frequently opposes for their apostasy (23:9–40; 28). They are prophesying by Baal, the Canaanite god of storms and fertility.
The courtroom metaphor is resumed (v. 5; Hos. 4:1; Mic. 6:1, 2).

Represent west and east, respectively. The appeal takes its meaning from the special position of Israel, namely their covenant with the Lord, and Jeremiah’s assertion that the nations’ gods are impotent. Yet other nations have been faithful to their so-called gods, while Israel and Judah abandoned the one true God.
See also Is. 1:2. Heaven and earth serve as witnesses of the covenant (Deut. 30:19; 31:28; 32:1).

Jeremiah stresses the seriousness of Judah’s sin.

**living waters.** God’s people have abandoned the source of living (that is, running) water in favor of stagnant cisterns that are not able even to retain the water that is in them. In contrast to the useless and empty idols, God alone provides life-giving water (Is. 55:1; John 4:10, 7:37–39).
Judah’s enemies (4:7), announcing desolation.

Egyptian cities. In Jeremiah’s era (specifically, 609–605 B.C.), Egypt and Babylon are contending over who will control Judah.

**crown.** Possibly a reference to Josiah, who is killed by Pharaoh Neco at the battle of Megiddo in 609 B.C. (2 Kin. 23:29).

One of Israel and Judah’s besetting sins has been to seek help from political alliances, rather than the Lord (Hos. 12:1).

**waters of the Nile ... Euphrates.** In light of v. 13, drinking the waters of the Nile, the main river of Egypt, or the Euphrates, the main river of Assyria, is a metaphor for Judah’s placing its hope for deliverance in one these nations or the other. Yet, like cracked cisterns, they have never delivered the aid that Judah anticipates.

See Deut. 12:2; 1 Kin. 14:23. These are typical sites of shrines to the gods of Canaan.

**whore.** Judah is portrayed as a harlot, unfaithful to the Lord (Ezek. 23:1–8; Hos. 3:1–5; 4:10–14).

The “vine” metaphor is frequently used for Israel, with God as the gardener who cares for the nation (12:10; Ps. 80:8–16; Is. 5:1–7; Ezek. 17:1–10). Jesus Christ is the true vine, and those who abide in Him are the branches (John 15:1–8).

**wild.** Lit. “foreign.” Foreignness here implies pagan religious practices.

Sin is only effectively washed away when there is repentance toward the Lord Himself as the One provides cleansing through the blood of the everlasting covenant (Is. 53:4–6; Heb. 9:11–15; 13:20).

**lye.** A powerful cleansing agent.

Probably refers to the Hinnom Valley, immediately south of Jerusalem, where abominable worship practices such as child sacrifice are occurring in Jeremiah’s era (7:31).

**young camel.** Characteristically irresolute and hard to direct, ready to follow any fresh impulse.
A picture of unrestrained lust. Instead of needing to be seduced by her lovers or to have her affections purchased, she herself has paid to pursue her foreign lovers.

The association of gods with particular localities is a distinguishing feature of pagan religion. These gods are fashioned out of wood and stone and are thus powerless (see 10:5), yet Judah ascribes real power to them.

Such forgetfulness is so unlikely as to be virtually impossible.

**my people have forgotten me.** See Is. 1:2, 3.

Refers to the persecution of the weak by the strong (a great theme of Amos; Amos 2:6–8; 4:1).

**you did not find them breaking in.** The Mosaic law gives homeowners the right to protect their own property against burglars (Ex. 22:2).
The nations from which Judah has sought aid against the Babylonians. They will be as much help as their impotent gods of wood and stone.
A posture for captives of war.

The bridal metaphor (2:2) now becomes one of divorce. According to the Mosaic law, a man is not permitted to remarry his divorced wife if in the meantime she has been married to another man (Deut. 24:1–4). How then could the northern kingdom of Israel take abundant lovers and think that she could simply return to her husband, the Lord, whenever she wished?
In Jeremiah’s day, prostitutes typically sit beside the road soliciting customers (see Gen. 38:14).
Northern Israel was disobedient to the terms of the covenant, so God withheld the necessary seasonal rainfall on which the harvest depended (see Deut. 11:14).

See Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion, and note on 1:2.

**Israel.** The northern kingdom was destroyed in 722 B.C.

**on every high hill and under every green tree.** Where the worship of the Canaanite fertility deities, Baal and Asherah, takes place in Jeremiah’s era. See note on 2:20.

**played the whore.** See theological note “Syncretism” on p. 1498.

See note on v. 1. The northern kingdom of Israel was “divorced” by being deported by Assyria (722 B.C.), an exile from which she did not return. Those events should provide a warning for the southern kingdom of Judah, but she is ignoring the warning even as Jeremiah is calling her to heed it.
See theological note “Syncretism” on p. 1498.

To those already deported by Assyria.

**Return, faithless Israel.** This call implies both repentance and a physical return to their territory, for these two aspects go together in Jeremiah’s message of salvation; see note on 29:14. Even though Israel was scattered for her faithlessness, she can still repent of her sins and be restored with a view toward having God grant her leaders who will feed (v. 15; lit. “shepherd”)her. How much more, then, can Judah hope to find forgiveness if she will only repent? Yet if Judah fails to repent in the face of the clear example of Israel’s judgment, it will demonstrate her to be even more stubborn and hard-hearted than Israel.

**I will not be angry forever.** This statement answers the question of v. 5; cf. 31:20.
Another use of the prostitution metaphor; see 2:20.

Lit. “I am your husband.” Even though the Lord has given His people a decree of divorce (v. 8), He remains committed to them.

**take ... one ... two.** God will save a remnant from among the exiles and bring them back to Zion, the place where His glory dwells in the temple (23:3 note; Is. 10:20–22 note).
Faithful kings like David (1 Sam. 13:14; Ezek. 34:23, 24), who will lead the people in the worship of the Lord.

These same words appear in reverse order in Gen. 1:28 (“Be fruitful and multiply”). God will make a new beginning with His people.

**in those days.** A future messianic age is now in view (cf. Is. 2:1–5).

**The ark ... shall not come to mind.** The importance of the ark will be diminished because the Lord will be present with His people in a new and more immediate way. The fact that “it shall not be made again” may suggest that it has already been destroyed by this time.

No longer is the ark the footstool of the Lord’s throne (Ex. 25:22; 1 Sam. 4:4). Now Jerusalem is itself the throne, indicating that the Lord rules the whole earth from the midst of His people (Zech. 2:10–12).
As a good Father, the Lord has longed to give a good heritage to His children. Yet their rebellion has made that impossible.
See 3:1; Hos. 1–3.
This summons parallels Hos. 14:4. The call to repentance goes further: the Lord Himself will enable the people to return (Deut. 30:6).
This loss of possessions and family is the antithesis of blessing (Deut. 7:13). Children are even being sacrificed to pagan gods (7:31).

This common oath formula invokes the Lord as witness to their commitments, as opposed to swearing by the name of some other deity. Such oaths must be performed in truth, justice, and righteousness. If Judah pursues such a lifestyle, it will be a source of blessing not merely for itself but for the surrounding nations as well, just as the Lord promised Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3).
The outward signs of ownership by the Lord are worth nothing unless they correspond to an inner reality. Only God can circumcise the heart (31:31–34; Deut. 10:16; 30:6).

A traditional method of raising an alarm by which a watchman warns the inhabitants of a city of impending danger (cf. Joel 2:1; Amos 3:6). Jeremiah begins to announce destruction at the hand of a foe from the north (see note on 1:13, 14). Fear of invasion will drive country-dwellers to the fortified cities for safety.
Traditional actions of indicating grief; cf. Jon. 3:5.

A day of reckoning when the things prophesied will come to pass (cf. Is. 2:11, 12). Instead of being the day of salvation for the Lord’s people, as they have hoped, it will be the day when He pours out His fierce anger.
The dry sirocco winds blow from across the desert and cause tremendous damage to crops.

These comparisons drawn from nature indicate the strength and speed of the enemy (cf. Is. 5:28). The invading army is not identified, perhaps because it is merely a tool of judgment in the hand of the Lord.
These northern locations will be among the first to see an invader from the north.
It is as if Judah’s enemies already own the land.
As representative of the people, the prophet himself feels deeply the pain that will come upon them.
This cry is common in psalms of lament (e.g., Ps. 13:1).

These are moral categories, not just intellectual categories. Original wickedness is strengthened by habit and practice (9:5). God’s people have become like children left to their own devices, children who will not learn to do what is right.

verse_quote: without form and void ... heavens . . . had no light.
note: Cf. Gen. 1:2, 14, 15. Creation itself is undone by His judgment.
The same phrase is used in Gen. 2:5. Again creation is being returned to its original chaos.
Covenant blessings are now reversed (Deut. 8:7–16).

A vivid repetition of the harlot metaphor. Instead of repenting and turning to the Lord, Judah has persisted in pursuing her former lovers, Assyria and Egypt, hoping in vain that they will provide deliverance for her.

**lovers ... seek your life.** These lines express the ironic truth of Judah’s self-deception.

Jerusalem is personified as a woman in labor (Lam. 1:6 note).

**Woe ... murderers.** Jerusalem utters her pathetic, dying breath.

verse_quote: if you can find ... pardon her.
note: This search is an allusion to Abraham’s prayer for Sodom (Gen. 18:22–32) and an implicit answer to Jeremiah’s prayer for the city (later forbidden; 7:16). But the city of Jerusalem is so totally corrupt that not even one righteous man can be found.

verse_quote: made their faces harder than rock.
note: The people’s determination not to repent is the chief frustration of the prophet (cf. Ezek. 3:7–9). This is not just the attitude of the poor and uneducated people but of the noble and powerful classes as well.

Such breach of God’s covenant brings the covenant curses of assault by wild animals on the people (Lev. 26:22). A person might possibly escape from one of these animals, but an attack by all three together will surely be fatal.
The motive for following false gods is the delusion that the gods of the land of Canaan have the power to make it fertile. The Lord claims the land’s fertility as His own sphere (Hos. 2:8, 9 notes).
Religious prostitution slips over into actual adultery in the worship of the fertility cults. See a similar description in 2:23, 24.
Again the courtroom metaphor is used; an appeal to witnesses is implied. The Lord’s justice must be accomplished.

This hint that punishment will not be final is one of several such clues in the early part of the book (12:14–17; 16:14, 15; and 23:3 note).

**are not the** LORD**’s.** In the same breath, Judah’s covenant status is annulled (Hos. 1:9 note). The apparently irreconcilable needs of judgment and salvation are both evident here.

Wrong belief about God is related to every kind of untruth (9:3–6).

**He will do nothing ... famine.** These words summarize the attitude of the people, reinforced by the oracles of the false prophets. See 28:2–4.
The people claim that far from having the Spirit (Hb. _ruah_), the prophets are but wind (also _ruah_).
That Judah’s enemies will consume the bounty of the land is a reversal of covenant blessing. See Deut. 7:13 for the promise of the very things now to be lost.

See Prov. 1:7.

**who have eyes ... hear not.** See note on Is. 6:10. The people become like the idols that they serve (Is. 44:18).

Jeremiah argues from God’s power in creation (Job 38–41; Rom. 1:18–20). The people’s folly is visible in their trust in powerless idols instead of fearing the all-powerful God, who truly controls the seasonal rains upon which their lives depend (see 3:3).
The nature of wickedness is to entice even the innocent into it. Prov. 2:12–19 describes its alluring speech.
Jeremiah moves from specifically religious sins to social evils, for the two are closely related.

This description symbolizes self-centered wealth, cf. Ps. 73:7.

**fatherless ... needy.** See note on Ps. 9:18. These people are often oppressed in Jeremiah’s day because they have no one to be their advocate.

verse_quote: my people love to have it so.
note: Not only are the prophets and priests teaching what was false, but such teachings are exactly what the people want. They want no one to confront them about their sinful behavior. Such comfort is shortsighted because it deliberately ignores what will happen in the end.

This territory bordering Jerusalem to the north is part of the southern kingdom of Judah. Normally, people would flee _to_ a fortified city in a crisis. In this case, Jerusalem is actually the most dangerous place to be, so people flee _from_ it.

**Tekoa.** A city in Judah, the home of Amos (Amos 1:1).

**Beth-haccherem.** An unknown location in Judah. Most likely, Tekoa and Beth-haccheremwere to the south and west of Jerusalem, so if an enemy from the north reaches them, he already has Jerusalem surrounded.

**north.** See note on 1:14.
See note on 2:2. Though a personification of Jerusalem (4:31 note), the simile has in mind the city’s refined women (Is. 3:16–26).
These “shepherds” are enemy officers with their troops (the “flocks”) taking possession of the land (cf. 4:15).
These are unusual times to attack; the enemy’s strength is such that he is free to attack whenever he likes., 5

A new oracle is addressed to the as-yet-unidentified force, which will act as the Lord’s instrument of judgment.

**oppression.** The rich and powerful of Jerusalem have oppressed their own people.
Judah cannot help pouring out her wickedness because that is her true nature (cf. Matt. 7:16).

Farmers are not supposed to glean everything but to leave something behind for the poor (Deut. 24:19–22). Babylon, however, may “glean” Judah completely (cf. 5:10). The Lord has deeper purposes behind the permission He gives (23:3 note). The curse is not absolute, for God does spare a small remnant to fulfill His covenant of redemption (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). See note on 11:23.
They are as deaf to the Lord’s word as uncircumcised pagans would be.

These opposites include everyone in between, showing that judgment will be as comprehensive as the spread of sin, which affects everyone in the community. The prophets and the priests, who are supposed to be the watchmen, are themselves implicated in the evil.

More than absence of war, peace means individual and social well-being that is the consequence of covenant-keeping. Repetition is a way of emphasizing something in Hebrew. The message of false prophets might be attractive but it cannot bring true peace (Mic. 2:6), whose counterpart is righteousness.
This phrase describes the traditional religious life of the Israelites from the time of Moses; it is the task of priests and prophets to direct the people.
The prophets (Is. 21:11; Ezek. 3:17; Hab. 2:1). Those few prophets who do faithfully declare the Lord’s word are ignored by the people.
See 2:4; Mic. 1:2.

Expensive ingredients used in religious rituals (Ex. 30:23–38). Sheba is located in distant southwest Arabia during Jeremiah’s era.

**burnt offerings are not acceptable.** This indictment is important in the Psalms and Prophets (Ps. 40:6–8; Is. 1:11–15; Mic. 6:6–8). Defiant, unrepentant sinning cannot simply be atoned for by the regular offerings (see Num. 15:30, 31; Matt. 23:23).
Those who seek to approach the Lord while their hearts are devoted to idols will not find access to Him (see Ezek. 14:1–5).

verse_quote: the north country ... the farthest parts of the earth.
note: Babylon (1:13, 14 note). From the perspective of those living in the Promised Land, Babylon is at the ends of the earth.

verse_quote: lay hold on bow and javelin ... on horses.
note: See the description of Babylon in Hab. 1:6–11. Though the Babylonians are God’s instrument, He does not approve of their cruelty.
A slogan that Jeremiah uses repeatedly (see 20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29). The mere report of the approach of such a fearsome enemy is utterly demoralizing.

verse_quote: mourning as for an only son.
note: Such mourning will be especially intense, as without a son the family’s name would be lost (see Zech. 12:10).
Elsewhere in the book, the Lord Himself is the One who tests both the people (9:7; 17:10; 20:12) and Jeremiah (11:20; 12:3). The prophet acts as God’s agent here (see Mal. 3:2, 3).
Lead is used in the process of refining silver. The process of refining Judah has yielded nothing of value.

Probably the gate leading to the inner court of the temple. Pilgrims may recite passages like Ps. 15 at this entry point to the temple, reminding one another of the need for purity among those who approach the presence of the Lord. Jeremiah stands in the central place of Judah’s worship to proclaim its falsehood. The power of this action is heightened because Jeremiah himself is a priest. Alternatively, the Lord may have chosen this location because of its exposure to numerous people.

**all you men of Judah ... to worship the** LORD**.** Possibly this prophecy is delivered on one of the great annual feasts (Ex. 23:14–18), for that is when every Israelite male is to be present.

verse_quote: Amend your ways and your deeds.
note:
OT believers were not saved by their works, but their actions revealed the true nature of their hearts (Matt. 7:16–18).

**this place.** The Promised Land. The force of Jeremiah’s appeal here, perhaps a shock to complacent Judah, is that they cannot take the land for granted.

verse_quote: deceptive words ... the temple of the
note: LORD**.** The repetition gives emphasis and sounds as if the worshipers view it as a magic formula that will automatically protect them. This false confidence in the inherent power of the temple to protect Jerusalem may stem in part from the Lord’s dramatic deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib and the Assyrian army in the days of Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:13–19:37). Some of the psalms also promise protection for the Lord’s city (e.g., Ps. 46), yet this promise cannot be disconnected from the need for God’s people to be faithful to their covenant commitments to the weakest members of the community.

verse_quote: if you ... to your own harm.
note:
The conditional language echoes that of the Mosaic covenant (Deut. 13:1–3; 14:28, 29). The law warns that if Israel breaks the covenant, she cannot expect the Lord’s protection but will be sent into exile (Deut. 28:25, 26).

**7:6 shed innocent blood.** This plea is not an exaggeration (19:4).
An allusion to five of the Ten Commandments (cf. Hos. 4:2), with a climactic stress on the first (Ex. 20:3).

verse_quote: this house, which is called by my name.
note:
See Deut. 12:5; 1 Kin. 8:43, where the “place” is identified as the Jerusalem temple.

**delivered.** False worship yields false security.
A secure place to which robbers return to divide their spoils. Jesus accused the Jerusalem temple of His own day of the same thing (Matt. 21:13).

Shiloh was a central place of worship for all Israel before David made Jerusalem the capital (Josh. 18:1; 1 Sam. 1:9). Since Shiloh is no more in Jeremiah’s day (it was probably destroyed by the Philistines because of the sins enumerated in 1 Sam. 2), it is a good demonstration of the prophet’s point that even a place where the Lord has made His name to dwell is not immune to His judgment. Just as the glory of God went into exile from Shiloh when the ark was captured (see 1 Sam. 4:22), so it can leave Jerusalem and go to those already in exile (see Ezek. 8–11). In that event, the city will be left unprotected. The same thing has happened already to the northern kingdom, the offspring of Ephraim (v. 15).

verse_quote: and when I spoke to you persistently.
note:
Lit. “and I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking,” which is meant to express the continuation of the action. Cf. 2 Chr. 36:15, 16.

**you did not listen.** An important theme in the book (6:17; 11:7, 8; 25:3; cf. 2 Kin. 17:13, 14). The statements in vv. 13–15 add a note of finality to the prophet’s message.

Such prohibition is ominous because one of the roles of the prophet is to intercede. (Abraham served as an intercessor and Moses did as well; cf. Gen. 20:7; Ex. 32:11–14.) The prohibition is repeated at 11:14 (cf. 15:1; 1 John 5:16). A key element in Jerusalem’s deliverance in the days of Hezekiah was the intercession of the prophet Isaiah (Is. 37:4–7).

A picture of the universal hold idolatry has on the people.

**queen of heaven.** A name for the Babylonian goddess Ishtar (44:19, 25). The cakes apparently bear her image (see 44:19).

verse_quote: man and beast ... fruit of the ground.
note: The worship of Ishtar, a fertility goddess, is supposed to ensure agricultural success. Yet a breakdown in the relationship between the Lord and His people will affect negatively the fertility of humans, their domestic animals, and all of their crops.

God is not interested in sacrifices without the inner worship of the heart; thus, the people might as well eat the sacrifices themselves if they offer them that way. This prophetic condemnation of empty ritual is all the more remarkable because the sacrificial system revealed to Moses is still in force in Jeremiah’s era. Jeremiah is not alone in speaking this way (cf. 1 Sam. 15:22, 23; Is. 1:11–15; Hos. 6:6; Amos 5:21–25; Mic. 6:6–8).

verse_quote: walked ... stubbornness of their evil hearts.
note: This portrayal of Judah strongly suggests a native disposition toward evil in the human heart. The word “stubbornness” in Hebrew may more properly be rendered “self-reliance.” Jeremiah uses this term more than any other biblical author.
See note on v. 13.

This command is in the grammatical feminine and personifies Jerusalem as a woman (cf. 2:1, 2). The Nazirite vow involves allowing the hair to grow unchecked as a sign of consecration to the Lord (Num. 6:2–8). The cutting off and throwing away of Jerusalem’s hair therefore represents her de-consecration and rejection by the Lord because of her defilement. The Lord has rejected and forsaken His previously chosen city.

This verse is evidence of the presence of a foreign cult in the temple itself, as under Manasseh (2 Kin. 21:7). Josiah removed the abomination, but it has been returned by the time this oracle is given, possibly in the time of Jehoiakim (Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion). Ezekiel also describes such defilement (Ezek. 8:3–12). Such practices explain Jeremiah’s reference to Judah’s persistent rebelliousness.

The usual name for pagan cult centers (2 Kin. 23:8, 9).

**Topheth.** Lit. “place of fire.” This is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, where children are sacrificed to the foreign god Molech in Jeremiah’s day. Offering the firstborn child is practiced by Israel’s neighbors in Jeremiah’s day, but in Israel the firstborn child is to be “redeemed” by substituting an animal for sacrifice (Ex. 13:2; 34:19, 20). Child sacrifice is expressly forbidden (Lev. 18:21; 20:2–5). See also 2 Kin. 23:10 and note. The reference may be meant to undercut a perverted notion among some that child sacrifice fulfills an ancient Mosaic custom (cf. Ex. 22:29).

**Valley of the Son of Hinnom.** Southwest of Jerusalem; its equivalent name in Greek is _Gehenna,_ or “hell” (Matt. 5:22 note).

See 1 Kin. 14:11 and note. Exhuming remains (8:1) inflicts an even greater dishonor than leaving a corpse exposed to scavengers, and it is a way of defiling sacred places so that they could no longer be used for that purpose (2 Kin. 23:16, 18).

verse_quote: spread before the sun ... moon ... host of heaven.
note: The irony in this curse is that they worship these heavenly bodies (2 Kin. 21:3–5). Is. 40:25, 26 declares the Creator to be greater than these created things.

verse_quote: Death shall be preferred to life.
note: Life in exile will be so traumatic that even death will be better (see Deut. 28:64–68).

Just as it is normal for people to get up again after they have fallen down, so ought it be normal for God’s people to repent when they sin. Yet instead of turning away from their sins and repenting, they have turned toward them in a headlong rush like a horse charging into battle.

The created order perfectly obeys the laws that God has laid out for it; thus, birds never refuse to migrate at the proper time. Yet the Lord’s people, who out of all humanity ought to be most obedient, do not know or obey His rules.
The wise are a group, perhaps the same group as the “scribes”; cf. 2 Sam. 8:17; Ezra 7:6 and notes. It is likely that the oral traditions of some scribes have in Jeremiah’s day distorted the law.

Unlike the wisdom expounded in Proverbs, the wisdom of these scribes is empty, having no real knowledge of the Lord’s Word. They may know what it says, but failing to do what it says betrays a lack of wisdom. See Deut. 4:6. The same was true of the scribes of Jesus’ day (see Matt. 23).

The motive for the false prophets is greed. If they pretend that there is no real problem in society and that there is peace between God and His people, they are more likely to be popular. See note on 6:14., 11

The vine symbolizes Judah (2:21). However, the language also suggests a loss of fertility, a blessing of God that the people have attributed to other gods (Hos. 2:8, 9). They will personally suffer the covenant curses, whose reality they have strenuously denied.

The word is the same as for “gathering” the harvest in v. 13. Yet there is no safety in numbers, even in the fortified cities. Once they understand that the Lord is judging them for their sin, it will be too late to repent. The ones who insist on seeking their water from broken cisterns (2:13) will be given poisoned water to drink. This recalls the judgment at Marah in the wilderness, where the water was too bitter to drink, though on that occasion the Lord graciously healed the water (Ex. 15:22–25).
This may be taken literally, as a kind of plague (cf. the “poisoned water,” v. 14; Num. 21:6), or as a figure of speech for the enemy.

verse_quote: My joy is gone; grief is upon me.
note: The Hebrew in this phrase is problematic; this rendering comes from the Septuagint (text note).
The false confidence of 7:10 has been shattered by unfolding events.
Jeremiah participates in the suffering of the people (14:2). Likewise, the Lord does not delight in the judgment of the wicked (see Ezek. 18:23).

Gilead is known for its medicinal products in Jeremiah’s day (46:11), but the balm that one could normally expect to find there is absent.

**no physician ... restored.** For the healing metaphor and false healers, see 8:11. The desire for a physician is an appeal to God as such; He will come at the right time in the person of Christ, the Great Physician (30:17; cf. Luke 4:18, 19).

A key interpretive question here is determining who is speaking. It seems that the Lord Himself is offering this lament, though it could also be from Jeremiah. In either case, Jesus shares the sympathy for the people expressed in these verses (Luke 19:41).
This statement is jolting, especially if God is the speaker; however, the grammatical form of the verb shows that the action has not taken place.

This is a military simile; their bow is falsehood, and they go out wielding it as if to battle. The focus of this section is the sins of the tongue.

**declares the** LORD**.** God concurs with Jeremiah’s estimation of the moral condition of the people (vv. 1, 2). The Lord’s attitude is expressed through the prophet.
See note on 6:27–30.
Such peace (Hb. _shalom_) is a true basis for society, and a product of covenant faithfulness; its opposite is falsehood, which is unfortunately the actual basis of their society.

Jeremiah weeps particularly for the desolation of the land God gave His people to be rich and populated, but which is desolate. See Mic. 1:8. The Lord also grieves for the destruction of the land, but justice must be done.
The lack of inhabi­tants marks the land as cursed (cf. Ps. 44:19; Is. 13:21, 22).
This language is reminiscent of the concept of wisdom as God-given knowledge (Prov. 1:2–5). The idea of wisdom as a recommendation of Israel among the nations (Deut. 4:6) has now been overturned.
See Deut. 4:8.

verse_quote: but have stubbornly followed their own hearts.
note: See note on 7:24. The people have developed an atrophy of the will by continually refusing to do what is right.

verse_quote: the nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known.
note: They are aware of their existence, but they have never had a relationship with them (cf. Deut. 28:36; Ezek. 32:9).
The weeping theme is taken up again (vv. 1, 10), with the OT’s clearest allusion to professional wailing women employed to lead in mourning for the dead (Amos 5:16).

The actions of death are poetically personified as a stealthy thief or a conquering army.

**children ... young men.** See 6:11; Lam. 5:13–15 and notes. Death usually carries off older people, but now it will remove the children and young men as well, leaving the community without hope for the future.

See theological note “Knowledge of Self and Knowledge of God.” Wisdom, might, and riches are natural places for sinful human beings to place their trust. Yet none of these things can withstand the outpouring of God’s wrath.

**9:24 understands and knows me.** See v. 12. Ultimately, wisdom is knowing God personally, not abstractly. The Christian’s boast is in the cross of Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 1:18–31).

**steadfast love, justice, and righteousness.** These three characteristic qualities of the Lord are revealed and exercised in the covenant.

verse_quote: circumcised merely in the flesh . . . uncircumcised in heart.
note:
See 4:4. Israel is outwardly circumcised, but inwardly uncircumcised. Some of the surrounding nations also practiced circumcision, but not as a covenant sign of belonging to the Lord. Because Israel and Judah are uncircumcised in their hearts, they are effectively in the same condition as the nations. Cf. Jer. 4:4, 6:10; Deut. 10:16, 30:6; Rom. 2:25–29; 4:9–12; 9:8; Gal. 5:6; 6:15.

**9:26 who cut the corners of their hair.** A pagan religious practice, forbidden to the Israelites (Lev. 19:27).

Terror characterizes the worship of false gods. Worship of heavenly bodies (8:2 and note) carries with it special fears related to the occurrence of unusual phenomena. A biblical understanding of creation should take away these fears, accepting such phenomena as God’s created order (Gen. 1; Is. 40:26). Yet God’s people can also be overawed by such events.
This word, used elsewhere by Jeremiah for idols (cf. v. 8), conveys their emptiness (2:5). They are as powerless to inflict harm as scarecrows are (v. 5).

Although some idols are cast in precious metals (Ex. 32:4; Neh. 9:18), more often they are carved out of wood and decorated with gold or silver as described here (Is. 40:18–20). The most common household idols are molded from clay and fired like pottery (Judg. 18:17; Is. 30:22; 42:17).

In contrast to the powerlessness of the idols, the Lord is great and mighty. The biblical fear of God involves more than the dread of God’s judgment. It includes awe, reverence, and adoration in response to God’s majesty and holiness (Ps. 2:11, 12).

**10:7 O King.** This appellation counters claims to kingship by false deities such as Bel (or Marduk) in Babylon (cf. Is. 46:1; 43:15).

**wise ones.** Their wisdom is contrasted with the Lord’s (v. 12).
The language is like that of the OT’s Wisdom Literature.

The former is in Spain, but Uphaz has not been identified. Since it is brought from such distant locations, presumably this silver and gold are of particularly fine quality. Violet and purple are colors associated with wealth and royalty because the dyes used to make them are especially expensive in Jeremiah’s era.

See Deut. 5:26.

**everlasting King.** See note on v. 7; cf. Ex. 15:18; 2 Sam. 7:13. The eternity of God’s kingdom is affirmed, even though the house of David is about to come to its historical end.

**wrath ... indignation.** Cf. Ps. 97:5.

verse_quote: The gods who did not make ... shall perish.
note: This verse is in Aramaic (text note), the international language of the period, and reflects the testimony to be delivered to the nations in a way they can understand. The saying also incorporates a play on the similar sound of “make” and “perish” in Aramaic_._

Jeremiah appeals to the power of the true God in creation in his argument against foreign gods. For creation’s being accomplished by God’s wisdom, see Prov. 8:22–31, a passage that foreshadows Christ as the preexistent wisdom of God (Col. 1:15; 2:3).

verse_quote: When he utters ... from his storehouses.
note: See Pss. 29:3, 4; 135:5–7. The Lord’s control of the rain directly counters claims made for the Canaanite god Baal (see 1 Kin. 17:1). God alone has power over rain, clouds, lightning, and wind.

For the Lord as one’s portion or inheritance, see Num. 18:20; Ps. 16:5. Originally this referred specifically to the Levites, but later it is used more broadly to describe what God promised Israel in His covenant with them. The same God who created the universe also summoned Israel into existence and gave them their land as an inheritance.

See Jeremiah’s cry in 4:19–21. He empathizes with his audience. The medical metaphor is a favorite in Jeremiah (6:7; 14:17; 30:12, 13, 15, 17). The exile is now inevitable; Judah’s wound is incurable.
The sorrows of losing children fill in the picture of the desolation of exile (16:3–5). The picture of Judah as a tent is also found in 4:20.
Not only are the idols and the ones who worship them stupid (cf. 10:14), but the leaders (“shepherds”) are as well (cf. 4:22 note).
Babylon (1:13, 14 note).
This thought is found also in the Wisdom Literature (Prov. 16:9).

verse_quote: in justice; not in your anger.
note: Distinguishes between a corrective chastening, as promised in 2 Sam. 7:14, 15, and a judgment that represents casting someone off forever (see Ps. 6:1)
This verse may be a citation of Ps. 79:6, 7.
Judah’s idolatry is a violation of the covenant and will result in captivity as part of the curses of the covenant.

The commands of God in the Mosaic covenant (Deut. 1:1). If the people were unfaithful to the Mosaic covenant, they would lose possession of the land, though their salvation was always a work of God’s grace.

**covenant.** A covenant is a solemn agreement between two or more parties. It is the kind of relationship into which God freely entered first with all mankind (Gen. 9:1–17), then with Abraham as the father of Israel (Gen. 17:1–21), then with Israel at Sinai (Ex. 19–24), then with David (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Ps. 89:3), and finally with the whole people of God in the new covenant (31:31–34 notes). The goal of the covenant is for the Lord to have a holy people belonging to Himself (see v. 4).
See Deut. 27:15–26.
Israel’s formative but painful experiences in Egypt.

verse_quote: confirm the oath that I swore.
note:
The covenant with Abraham was in the form of a divine promise (Gen. 15:17–21; cf. Deut. 4:31). Under the terms of the Mosaic covenant, the temporal blessings of the Abrahamic covenant (i.e., the possession of the land) were administered on the basis of Israel’s obedience (Ex. 19–24; Lev. 26; Deut. 28), but the Abrahamic blessing of eternal salvation was administered in the same way it is administered under the new covenant—on the basis of Christ’s obedience. Under both covenants, the obedience of believers demonstrates the vitality of their professed faith; it is not the means by which they secure their righteousness before God (Rom. 3:21–26; James 2:14–26).

**a land flowing with milk and honey.** See Ex. 3:8; Deut. 6:3.

**So be it.** Hb. _amen_. Indicates acceptance of the terms laid down. See Deut. 27:15–26.
For the blessings that accompany obedience to the Sinai covenant and the curses for disobedience, see Lev. 26 and Deut. 28., 8
This could be resistance to the Lord’s words through Jeremiah, or opposition to Josiah’s reform. Either way, the word “conspiracy” has overtones of rebellion against a king (see 2 Kin. 15:30; 17:4).
Again, the covenant is traced back to the promise to the patriarchs (v. 5 and note). Judah’s present breach of it is consistent with the pattern of Israel’s history (see esp. the book of Judges).

verse_quote: I will not listen to them ... they cannot save them.
note: When the inevitability of judgment finally dawns on Judah, the people will cry out to the Lord, only to find Him deaf to their pleas. When they cry out to their idols, they will discover that they are unable to help them., 12
Incense was used in pagan worship and also in worship of the Lord (1:16; 7:9; 18:15; Ex. 30:7–9). It was one of the simplest offerings to make and could be offered in a variety of locations.
Since the Lord already determined that He would judge His people, there is no point in Jeremiah’s interceding for them. See note on 7:16.

Judah, also in 12:7. The term of endearment is in line with the courtship and bridal imagery of 2:2; 3:1.

**in my house.** See 7:10, 11; Ezek. 8:6–13.

**sacrificial flesh ... exult.** The Hebrew is difficult; the criticism, however, is of unacceptable worship that produces a falsely based joy in God’s salvation.
The Lord had planted and provided for Israel in a way that should have established her fruitfulness. However, she had turned out dry and barren. Paul uses a similar image for Israel in Rom. 11:17–24.

verse_quote: like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter.
note:
A simile drawing on the practice of sacrifice (see Ps. 44:11). Jeremiah often uses the language of the psalms of lament (see Introduction to the Psalms). As a type of Christ, Jeremiah prefigures the sufferings of Christ in his life (Is. 53:7).

**tree with its fruit.** Meaning Jeremiah and his message, or an emphatic reference to his life.

**cut him off ... remembered no more.** Not to be remembered, by having no children, is the worst of fates for the people of Jeremiah’s day. Those who tried to cut off Jeremiah’s remembrance are themselves forgotten, while through his prophecy, Jeremiah is remembered today.

Jeremiah is not asking for the Lord to judge his personal enemies but for the Lord to establish His justice in the face of attempts by the wicked to suppress it, which is a common theme in the psalms of lament (e.g., Ps. 78:9, 10). See Introduction to the Psalms: Special Issues: The Curses of the Psalms.

They are from Jeremiah’s own town (1:1). The details of the plot reveal that his worst opposition comes from those closest to him (Ps. 69:7–9; Matt. 10:36, citing Mic. 7:6). In this respect also, Jeremiah prefigures Christ (John 7:2–5; Acts 1:15–20).
This threat of total extinction contrasts the fate of those who plot against Jeremiah, the Lord’s chosen prophet, with that of Judah in general (see 4:27; 5:10; 6:9, and notes).

–**3 Why does the way of the wicked prosper.** The psalmist asks the same question in Pss. 37 and 73. Here, instead of pleading the Lord’s case against the people, the prophet pleads his own case with the Lord. Since God is sovereign, the wicked must have been planted by Him (see 1:10). They are growing like a green tree, while Jeremiah himself continues to suffer.

The Lord gently rebukes Jeremiah by making comparisons from the lesser to the greater, from what is easy to what is comparatively more difficult. If the prophet is struggling now, what will he do when the opposition to him gets much greater?

verse_quote: your brothers and the house of your father.

note:
God’s “heritage” includes both the land given to Israel (Deut. 4:21) and the people themselves. See vv. 8, 9; 2:7.

**beloved.** See 11:15 and note.

This first of a series of similes (cf. vv. 9, 10) shows how Judah’s nature has been changed.

**I hate her.** As often in the Bible, “hate” is the only alternative to love (Mal. 1:2, 3). It includes the action that flows from the feeling, not merely the feeling itself.

Foreign rulers.

**pleasant portion.** See Is. 5:7.

verse_quote: The whole land is made desolate.
note: The land of Canaan, once the royal garden of God has been turned into a desert.
The verse exposes the lie of the prophets’ false proclamations of peace (6:14).

Though the Lord uses Judah’s enemies to punish her, these foes themselves will also be judged.

**pluck up.** When God judges Judah’s enemies by removing them from their own lands, He also will deliver and restore Judah. Chs. 30–33 develop this theme.

verse_quote: after I have plucked them up ... his land.
note: This marks an astonishing turn in thought, anticipating a restoration and salvation of all the peoples of the world. Jeremiah looks forward to the inclusion of the Gentiles in God’s salvation (46:26; 48:47; 49:6), as do other prophets (e.g., Is. 42:6). The promise of the Abrahamic covenant cannot be nullified by Israel’s disobedience; God is determined to bless all nations through Abraham and his seed.

verse_quote: they shall be built up ... my people.
note: See Is. 19:25 for an equally surprising use of “my people”—for Egypt.

The loincloth symbolizes the close relationship between God and His people. Linen is expensive in Jeremiah’s day, so this is a costly garment. Several of the prophets, especially those called to address hostile audiences such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel, perform these kinds of sign-acts that are designed to display their message in pictorial form .

A nearer location than the river in Mesopotamia may be intended (possibly Parah, Josh. 18:23, which is close to Anathoth). The similarity of name nevertheless suggests the Euphrates and therefore the Babylonian exile.
The loincloth’s predictable ruin depicts the corruption of the people, who are no longer fit for a relationship with the Lord—or anything else for that matter.

verse_quote: made the whole house ... cling to me.
note: The Lord spells out the meaning of the symbolic act as an illustration of His covenant with all Israel.

Wine is here used as a symbol of God’s wrath (25:15–29). As with the sign-act, the parable depicts an obvious truth and then applies it to Judah’s situation. The leaders of Judah will be filled with drunkenness and then smashed against one another like clay wine jars, destroying them in the process.

verse_quote: to the king and the queen mother.
note:
Probably Jehoiachin and his mother, Nehushta (2 Kin. 24:8). This prophecy is thus close to the time of Nebuchadnezzar’s attack on Jerusalem in 597 B.C. (Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion). The queen mother exercises a position of power and influence in society (1 Kin. 15:13). The poem takes the form of a lament, acting as if they are already dead.

**has come down.** See 22:24–26. This judgment spells the end of the Davidic dynasty, and seems to conflict with the promise to David (2 Sam. 7). However, see 33:14–26 for the future fulfillment of the Davidic covenant.

These cities along the southern border will be the last to see the Babylon invaders, who will approach from the north. If they are surrounded, the whole country is overrun. Judah’s pride in her own resources is hollow (v. 17).
See 4:6.
A picture of public shame, as of a prostitute or an adulteress. The punishment fits the crime (see 3:8, 9). Compare the similar judgment on the Lord’s adulterous people in Ezek. 16:36 and Nah. 3:5.

A rhetorical question expecting a negative answer. Ethiopians in the Bible come from Cush, the southern part of Egypt, and have dark skin. It is typical of Jeremiah to assert Judah’s inability to repent and obey the Lord—hence his new covenant theology (31:31–34 and notes). See theological note “Free Will” on p. 1293.

Recalls the lot cast for the division of the land (Josh. 14:2). Now it signifies expulsion from the same land.

**lies.** “The lie” is a common derogatory term for idols.

The people are so hardened in their sin that God will not answer Jeremiah’s prayer for deliverance from the punishment of drought, the sword, famine, and plague—four of the covenant curses threatened in Lev. 26:19–26. In answer to Jeremiah’s question as to whether God has rejected Judah completely (14:19), God replies that the coming judgment is inevitable because of Judah’s sin, but He assures Jeremiah of personal deliverance from his enemies.

**14:1The word of the LORD that came.** This is not the normal Hebrew phrase that introduces a prophetic oracle, for the first part of this chapter is more of a lament over the drought than specific instructions from the Lord.
A sign of mourning.
The Lord either gives or withholds the rain (Deut. 11:10–15; 28:12).
These hardy wild animals are used to withstanding the normal variations in rainfall in the Promised Land. However, even they will be unable to survive the drought., 6
The Hebrew word also means “pool,” a striking word in time of drought.

This calling explains the meaning of “for your name’s sake” in v. 7. The Lord’s honor is at stake in the fortunes of His people. Yet they cannot simply assume that He will always rescue them from trouble, no matter how they have behaved.

LORD**.** God responds directly to the prayer of vv. 7–9. Often in a lament, there is an assurance of deliverance after confession and supplication. In this case, however, since there is no real repentance, the Lord responds by confirming the judgment against them.

**this people.** Significantly, God does not use “my people.”
See 7:16 and note. Here the prohibition follows the intercession in vv. 7–9.

verse_quote: fast ... burnt offering and grain offering.
note:
Ritual for its own sake—even ritual ordained by God Himself—does not move God (7:21–23 note).

**sword ... famine ... pestilence.** The first of fifteen appearances of this combination in Jeremiah (e.g., 15:2). This is a typical summation of the horrors that judgment can bring (Deut. 32:24, 25).
Those who falsely prophesy peace (6:1–4; 8:11). Jeremiah pleads on behalf of the people whom they have misled.

The prophet’s plea (v. 13) misses its mark: the people should have tested the prophets by their prophecies (Deut. 13:2, 3; 18:21, 22). Jeremiah’s own words are themselves tragically vindicated by the events surrounding Jerusalem’s fall.

**none to bury.** See 7:33.

verse_quote: Let my eyes run down with tears.
note: The prophet’s sorrow represents the Lord’s heartbreak over having to judge His own people in this way, just as Jesus later weeps over hard-hearted Jerusalem (Matt. 23:37). The prophet laments the way in which God’s people have changed from a virgin daughter to a wanton prostitute. However, there are no tears of repentance in the eyes of those to whom the prophet speaks.
Because of the false prophets’ teaching (v. 13 and note).

The temple is in view (see 2 Kin. 19:15; cf. 1 Kin. 8:27).

**your covenant.** Jeremiah recalls the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen. 15:12–21; 26:3–5; 28:13–15; Lev. 26:42–45).

God identifies two great prophets who were archetypal intercessors for Israel (Ex. 32:11–14; 1 Sam. 12:23). Note also Elijah in 1 Kin. 17:1. Prayer for the people is again prohibited (7:16; 11:14), and the prayer just offered (vv. 19–22) is specifically rejected.
See 1 Kin. 21:23; note on 7:33.

A son of the reformer King Hez­ekiah (2 Kin. 20:21) and one of the most wicked kings (2 Chr. 33:1–9). Even after the reforms of his grandson Josiah, Judah’s punishment and exile continues to be linked to him (2 Kin. 23:26). See Introduction: Author; Date and Occasion.

The people claim that God has rejected them (14:19), but the reality is the exact opposite. The phrasing in the Hebrew is emphatic: “_You_ [the people] have rejected me.”

**going backward.** See 3:22.

**I am weary of relenting.** Such promises as in 31:20 are for the moment in the background.

Winnowing involves separating the grain from the chaff by throwing both into the air with a special fork; the lighter chaff is blown away by the wind, while the heavier grain falls to the ground. See 4:11, where the metaphor is used slightly differently. Here it means punishment (cf. Is. 41:16).
The Babylonians are so confident that they don’t try to conceal their plans but attack in broad daylight (see 6:4).

A picture of blessing (Ps. 127:5) is reversed.

**rest of them ... to the sword.** Even the remnant left by the destruction is threatened with death. Cf. Is. 6:13, where a similar thought is finally softened by the promise of the “seed.”

These words describe the role that has been assigned to Jeremiah as the prosecutor of the Lord’s case against His people (see 2:9).

**I have not lent ... borrowed.** Lending money at interest is forbidden in Ex. 22:25, but was nonetheless a common exploitative practice in antiquity. If Jeremiah has taken advantage of people in that way, or has borrowed money and been unable to repay it, people will have good reason to hate him (Prov. 22:7). The people’s hatred for him, therefore, is groundless.

How can Jeremiah be expected to change Judah’s stubborn heart? See 13:23 and note, as well as 28:10–13.

**from the north.** Babylon, Judah’s enemy, will come from the north (see 1:13, 14).
This prophecy is fulfilled for Jeremiah at 43:4–7.

Recalls the sweet side of the bittersweet task of receiving God’s words (Ezek. 3:1–3).

**I am called by your name.** This phrase is applied to the people in 14:9.

No doubt this is literally true, partly due to his enforced celibacy (16:2). But there can also be a profound sense of loneliness for the unwelcome prophet; cf. Elijah in 1 Kin. 19:10 and Jesus in Matt. 26:37, 38.

**indignation.** When he ate the scroll—i.e., received God’s words—the prophet internalized the Lord’s anger toward His people. Cf. note on v. 16.

The wound is Judah’s in 14:17. The whole phrase is applied to Judah in 30:12, together with a promise of healing (30:16, 17). See also 10:19, where it is used of Jeremiah.

**a deceitful brook.** Jeremiah accuses the Lord of behaving like an unreliable stream that dries up during the summer months when there is no rain (see 20:7).

Jeremiah is prohibited from marrying and taking part in other normal activities as a sign of coming judgment (ch. 16). A sharp contrast is drawn between the destinies of those who trust in people and those who trust in God (17:1–18).

verse_quote: You shall not take a wife.
note: The prohibition is related exclusively to Jeremiah’s role as a prophet of Judah’s fate (1 Cor. 7:26). Even priests and those who take Nazirite vows are normally free to marry in the prophet’s era. Jeremiah will be childless, a sign that there is no immediate future for Judah. A day is coming when many who have married will lose their spouses and children in the Babylonian invasion.
See note on 14:12.

verse_quote: Do not enter the house of mourning.
note: In the coming judgment on Jerusalem, so many people will die that normal funeral practices will be suspended. Jeremiah is to act out the Lord’s lack of compassion toward His people.

verse_quote: cut himself or make himself bald.
note: These pagan practices are forbidden in Deut. 14:1. Such paganism has become so common in Judah that it must be specifically banned in this passage.
After v. 2 and v. 5, there is yet a third symbolic prohibition.
See also 7:34. Such sounds are typical of times of peace and hope (Matt. 24:38, 39; cf. 33:10, 11).

Jeremiah’s extraordinary behavior is intended to provoke people to ask questions about the causes of the coming judgment. The answer is a combination of the sins of the fathers (14:20) and the even greater sins of the present generation (31:29, 30; Ezek. 18:2–4).

verse_quote: hurl you out of this land.
note:
God will send them into exile (see Deut. 28:36, 64).

**serve other gods.** With a punishment to fit the crime, the people who have served other gods in the land the Lord gave them will be made to serve these same gods in the homelands of those gods. There, the people will finally discover that these gods can provide no benefit.

Judah is pictured as the prey of the Lord.

**every mountain and every hill ... clefts of the rocks.** There will be no escape (23:24; Is. 2:19).
This is normally be good news for God’s people. See theological note “The Omniscience of God” on p. 1041. Here, however, it means inescapable judgment.
The Hebrew word for “double” may mean an exact match, in the same way that one might speak of an actor’s “double.”

ORD, **my strength.** Unlike the rest of God’s people, Jeremiah still finds refuge in the Lord. The nations too will ultimately reject their own gods (“the lies”; 13:25 note) and come to the Lord, underlining the extreme foolishness of Judah’s continuing commitment to her idolatry.

verse_quote: know that my name is the
note: LORD**.** Knowing the Lord’s name here means recognizing His authority and power through His acts of judgment.

Judah’s heart of stone is so hard that only a tool of the hardest material can possibly write on it.

**on the tablet of their heart.** This metaphor recalls tablets for writing laws. See 31:33, where the law will be written on the heart, and Prov. 3:3; 7:3. In the new covenant, Christ writes the law on His people’s hearts by His Spirit (2 Cor. 3:3).

**on the horns of their altars.** These altars should commemorate atonement for sin, but where the sin is unforgiven, they continue to remind God of the sin itself.
See notes on 2:20; Ex. 34:13; Deut. 7:5. Asherim are living trees or wooden poles in pagan sanctuaries that represent the fertility goddess Asherah.
In Jeremiah’s era, pagan worship takes place on “high places” such as mountaintops. However, in some cases, the high places are located within towns and cities.

verse_quote: heritage that I gave to you.
note: The Promised Land (2:7).
Two different Hb. words for “man” are used here. The second word (_adam_) focuses on the weakness of mere humanity in contrast to the power of God (cf. Ezek. 28:2).
The Lord repays trust because He is by nature trustworthy (Is. 7:9). The close similarity between vv. 7, 8 and Ps. 1:1–3 suggests that trust in the Lord entails obedience to His law.
This image is a potent symbol of strength in a dry country, and a reminder that true fertility is to be found in the Lord’s blessing, not in the Canaanite fertility gods Baal and Asherah (Ps. 1:3).
In the OT, the “heart” is more than the seat of emotion. It represents the basis of character, including the mind and the will (4:19; Prov. 4:23; 16:23). See theological note “Free Will.”

Lit. “kidneys.” In ancient Hebrew idiom, these organs represent the seat of the emotions. Together with “heart,” “mind” indicates a person’s secret thoughts and feelings. No human being can completely uncover someone else’s thinking, but the Lord weighs every secret intention and is able to dispense perfect justice to all. Given the corrupt state of every human heart, it is not good news that the Lord will judge each one according to the fruit of his or her deeds.

In the prophet’s day, people commonly believe that partridges steal the eggs of other birds, but the hatchlings return to their natural parents. In the same way, a person will not be able to retain riches unjustly gained.

**and at his end ... fool.** On the transience of riches, see Prov. 23:4, 5. In the Bible, “fool” indicates someone with a moral deficiency, not a mental one.

See note on 14:21; Ps. 99:1.

**from the beginning.** This implies that Zion was chosen as God’s throne even before the temple was built (Ex. 15:17). The mountain where the temple was built was the same one on which Abraham was to offer up Isaac (Gen. 22:2; 2 Chr. 3:1).

They will soon be forgotten. Cf. the thought of Ex. 32:32.

**the fountain of living water.** See 2:13.
The psalmist sometimes uses the language of sickness to describe broader difficulties and trials. The Lord’s deliverance from such trials comes as healing.

verse_quote: Where is the word of the
note: LORD**.** With this taunt, Jeremiah is accused of being a false prophet (Deut. 18:21, 22), though he has been a faithful shepherd and not a hireling. See Mic. 7:10; 2 Pet. 3:2–4.

Prayer for judgment upon his enemies is common in Jeremiah (11:20; 12:3; 15:15). The words are reminiscent of his call (1:17).

**double destruction.** See note on 16:18.
This location is not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture.
The message is given at the gates because of their role in commerce (see Neh. 13:15, 19).

Carrying a load is forbidden on the old covenant Sabbath since it is a form of work. Bringing loads through the gates of Jerusalem necessitates further work in the form of selling on the Sabbath.

**keep the Sabbath day holy.** Specific appeal is made to the Sabbath commandment, which is a central requirement of the Lord’s covenant with His people, distinguishing them from their neighbors (Ex. 20:8–11; Deut. 5:12–15; Neh. 10:31; Is. 56:2). The exile is in part a punishment for Israel’s failure to keep the Sabbath, as well as an opportunity for the land to enjoy its Sabbath rest (see Lev. 26:34, 35; 2 Chr. 36:21).

This prophecy presents a picture (partly repeated in 22:4) of the restoration of the Davidic dynasty, the social structure, and the worship, which all center on the temple. See also 23:5, 6; 30:9; 33:14–26. All that is threatened for Judah, therefore, can be reversed.

**17:26 the Shephelah ... the hill country . . . the Negeb.** The agricultural regions to the west and south of Jerusalem.

Just as a potter remolds a marred pot, God will remold His people by disciplining them in exile (18:1–17). Jeremiah portrays God’s judgment by breaking a clay jar (ch. 19), and he is mistreated because of his unpopular message (18:18–23; ch. 20).
Apparently in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, near the Potsherd Gate (19:2); hence the command to “go down.” See also 7:31.
The potter has freedom with respect to his plans. The spoiling of his first intention is not final.
The analogy with Israel follows. The use of “Israel” recalls God’s historic purposes of election for the whole people, purposes to which Judah is now heir.

verse_quote: If at any time ... I will relent.
note: The potter illustration (vv. 2–4) shows that the Lord’s purposed judgment may be revoked by that nation’s repentance. Judah cannot rest simply in being the Lord’s chosen people if by her actions she continues to rebel against Him. From one perspective, the Lord does not change His mind, for He is unchanging and outside of time (Num. 23:19). Yet human actions of faithfulness, repentance, or rebellion have meaning and significance nonetheless., 8

The people’s hard-heartedness is demonstrated by their refusal to repent even when Jeremiah pleads with them. They would rather remain committed to their rebellion and perish than turn to the Lord and live. However, the prophet’s words also contain a message of hope for the next generation: even in exile, they can repent and receive the Lord’s blessing.

See note on 14:17.

**very horrible thing.** One of the strong terms used for idolatry (v. 15; cf. 5:30).
The slopes of the mountains in Lebanon are always covered with snow, and the waters that flow from them never run dry. In terms of faithfulness and consistency, Judah has been the exact opposite.

See note on 11:13.

**ancient roads ... side roads, not the highway.** See note on 6:16. The “side roads” are narrow and dangerous.
A gesture of astonishment and mockery.

Cf. 4:11.

**my back, not my face.** Withheld favor (2:27). God will turn His back on them.

The Lord’s claim in v. 12 that the people prefer their own plots or plans to obeying the Lord proves true; instead of repenting in response to the prophet’s words, the people plan to harm him.

**priest ... wise ... prophet.** Three means of receiving the Lord’s wisdom are through the teaching of the Mosaic law (priests; Deut. 33:8–11), reflection on God’s creation (wise men), and the declaration of the word of the Lord (prophets). The people are denying that the Lord has really turned His back on them, as Jeremiah maintains in v. 17.

This is legal language. Jeremiah’s opponents are not merely slandering him with their tongues but are plotting to kill him (v. 23). Anyone who brings a false charge against someone else, such as accusing Jeremiah of being a false prophet, is subject to the penalty they seek for him (see Deut. 19:18, 19).

verse_quote: Should good be repaid with evil.
note:
Cf. Ps. 35:12; 1 Pet. 2:19–24.

**dug a pit.** They have a murderous intention (v. 22). See Jeremiah’s actual experiences in 37:16; 38:6.

**stood before you ... for them.** See note on 15:1.
The word for flask in Hebrew (_baqbuq_) is onomatopoeic, mimicking the sound of liquid being poured from a long, narrow-necked decanter of some sort.

verse_quote: Valley of the Son of Hinnom.
note:
See note on 18:2.

**Potsherd Gate.** A gate on the south of the city, possibly the Dung Gate (Neh. 2:13). It may be where potters deposit their broken wares, which makes it an appropriate location for the sign.
The words closely resemble 2 Kin. 21:12, which also concerns judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The judgment is severe and shocking to anyone who hears of it.
Child sacrifice is more often related to the worship of the god Molech in the OT, but here it is linked to the worship of the Canaanite fertility god, Baal.
See note on 7:31.

verse_quote: I will make void the plans of Judah and Jerusalem.
note:
The Hebrew verb for “make void” has the same root as “flask” in v. 1, and thus again is onomatopoeic (lit., “I will empty”). Additionally, the Hebrew word for “plans” is used in 18:18 for the “counsel” that Judah expects to continue from the wise and in 18:23 for their “plotting” to kill Jeremiah. Another term is used for “plans” or “plots” in 18:11, 12, 18.

**the birds of the air and to the beasts of the earth.** Deut. 28:26 threatens the curse of dead bodies’ being left exposed to the birds and wild animals (cf. 7:33). Scholars have shown how important a proper burial was to the ancient Israelites. Therefore, this is an ultimate dishonor (cf. 2 Kin. 23:13–16, 19, 20).
**a thing to be hissed at ... and will hiss.** Jeremiah frequently combines noun and verb forms from the same Hebrew root in the same verse. This stylistic device is a common feature of his writing.

verse_quote: eat the flesh ... of his neighbor.
note: Such a horror occurs during the siege of 586 B.C. (Lam. 2:20 and note).

verse_quote: Then you shall break the flask.
note: The climax of the scene is another symbolic prophetic action (13:1–11 and notes). The earthenware flask shatters on impact (Ps. 2:9). The metaphor is familiar to the residents of the ancient world whom Jeremiah is to address.

Unlike the soft clay of ch. 18, Judah is so set in her ways that she cannot be reshaped (lit., “healed”) but only destroyed.

**Men shall bury ... no place else to bury.** See 7:32.

See 8:2 and note; also 2 Kin. 23:4, 5. This probably relates to the worship of the Astarte/Ishtar, the “queen of heaven” (7:18, 19).

**defiled like the place.** Josiah defiled Topheth (2 Kin. 23:10).

LORD**’s house.** Jeremiah repeats his main message in the temple in Jerusalem to ensure that it reaches a wider audience, triggering immediate opposition from the priests who are in charge of the temple.

The name is apparently common (cf. 21:1; 38:1, each text possibly referring to a different man). Note that senior priests are among Jeremiah’s audience in the valley (19:1), and Pashhur is perhaps among them.

Pashhur’s duties as governor of the temple include restraining those whose actions disrupt temple worship (29:26; Deut. 25:2, 3). Yet he does nothing about the idolatrous practices that Jeremiah identifies in 7:30, all the while persecuting the prophet by having him beaten and confined. Jeremiah’s prayer in 15:18 shows that faithful prophetic preaching is dangerous.

**the prophet.** This title affirms Jeremiah’s status as a true prophet, despite the legal action against him.

**the upper Benjamin Gate.** A prominent gate into the temple.

–**6 Terror on Every Side.** See 6:25. The people should be afraid to be associated with Pashhur, because he is a highly visible example of why the Lord’s anger is falling on them. He has abused God’s prophet openly while tolerating false prophets. As a result, he and his companions will become living examples of the truth of Jeremiah’s threats of exile.

Jeremiah did not foresee the trials that his task would bring, and he received his call (esp. perhaps 1:7, 8) as an overpowering compulsion (4:10). He laments his struggles in prayer, wrestling with God, his enemies, and himself. In saying that God has deceived him, he uses the same verb used of the Lord’s strategy in using false prophets to tell King Ahab what he wanted to hear (1 Kin. 22). However, God is not using Jeremiah like one of those false prophets but rather like Micaiah, telling the painful truth to those who do not want to listen.
A compulsion he cannot control makes him utter his message of coming wrath (see Amos 3:8; 1 Cor. 9:16; 2 Cor. 5:14).
See 6:25. If Jeremiah were deceived and his message were false, then the authorities could act against him.

As is typical in laments, the prophet turns from describing the difficulty of his situation to expressing his confidence in God’s power and protection. He anticipates that the Lord will act to vindicate him.

Unlike Jeremiah’s earlier laments (11:18–20; 15:10), this time there are no words from the Lord designed to encourage Jeremiah. He feels alone in his depression. Normally the person who brings a father the good news of the safe arrival of a baby boy is blessed, but here the prophet curses him. The Spirit has permitted this record of Jeremiah’s near-total despair to be preserved for the encouragement and consolation of believers in Christ: great faith is not incompatible with deep struggles. The prophet’s words are like Job’s (Job 3:1–26).
Sodom and Gomorrah, whose fate is proverbial (Gen. 18; 19; cf. Is. 1:9; Amos 4:11).

These chapters narrate the end of the Davidic dynasty, making it clear that disaster and exile are God’s judgment on the sins of Judah’s kings and people. Jeremiah denounces false prophets who lead the people astray (ch. 23), but also sounds a note of hope as God promises to gather a remnant of His people from captivity under the leadership of “a righteous Branch” from David’s house (23:3–8). The twin messages of judgment and future restoration are repeated in Jeremiah’s vision of two baskets of figs (ch. 24).

**21:1 Zedekiah.** The name means “the Lord is my righteousness.” See note on 1:2.

**sent to him.** Zedekiah maintains a vacillating dependence on Jeremiah without the moral courage to obey his warnings (37:3, 21; 38:5, 14, 19, 24–26). Having been placed on the throne by the Babylonians, he has only a tenuous hold on power, especially after he rebels against them.

**Pashhur.** Not necessarily the same Pashhur as in 20:1 (see note) or 38:1.

**Zephaniah.** A priest and the son of Maaseiah (29:25, 29; 37:3; 52:24), not the same as the prophet Zephaniah (Zeph. 1:1). In 2 Kin. 25:18, he is called “the second priest.”

A request for guidance. Not all such inquiries are sincere attempts to seek the Lord (see Ezek. 20:1–3).

**Nebuchadnezzar.** King of Babylon, 605–562 B.C. His name is formed with “Nabu” (or “Nebo”), a Babylonian god (Is. 46:1; Dan. 1:1). The variant form “Nebuchadrezzar” (text note) matches the Babylonian spelling more closely.

**making war against us.** Zedekiah has been a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar (37:1), but he rebels against Babylon in 589 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar finally lays siege to Jerusalem in 587.

**wonderful deeds.** The miraculous works of the Lord in the past for His people, perhaps especially His deliverance of Jerusalem from the Assyrians in the days of Hezekiah (see 2 Kin. 18, 19).
Chaldea is part of Babylon and the home of the dynasty founded by Nebuchadnezzar’s father, Nabopolassar. For this reason, “Chaldeans” sometimes serves as an alternative name for the Babylonians.

verse_quote: I myself will fight against you ... outstretched hand ... strong arm.
note:
The language depicts the Lord’s power in war, especially during the exodus, now horrifyingly turned against His people (Deut. 4:34; 5:15; 7:19; Amos 5:18).

**anger ... fury ... great wrath.** See Deut. 29:23.
See note on 14:12.

verse_quote: I set before you the way of life and the way of death.
note: In Deut. 30:19, Israel is given the choice between long life in the land if she obeys the Lord or exile if she is disobedient. However, since the people and their fathers have already chosen the way of disobedience and death, the choice for Jeremiah’s generation is simply between death for those who remain in Jerusalem and exile for those who surrender to the Babylonians.

verse_quote: for harm and not for good.
note: In contrast to the Lord’s good plans for those already in exile (29:11).
Now begins a section of oracles directed toward the last kings of Judah.
See 9:24. This requirement of justice is expected both of the earthly king and the messianic King (23:5; 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kin. 3:28; Ps. 72:1, 2).
The residents of Jerusalem are confident in its inaccessible location, yet they will find their confidence misplaced, as the Jebusites did before them (2 Sam. 5:6, 7).

A word for any of the kings, serving as the prelude to a demonstration of their virtually unbroken failure. They sit on David’s throne but they do not follow his example. As in 17:25, the future of the Davidic dynasty is tied to the faithfulness of the nation’s kings.

verse_quote: the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow.
note: Three of the most powerless groups in the community, whom the kings must protect (Ex. 22:22–24).

See Gen. 22:16; Is. 45:23 and notes.

**this house.** See 2 Sam. 7, where the promise was first made to David. “House” can refer to David’s family as well as to a physical building.
These are fertile regions (cf. 8:22 and note). In the prophet’s day, Lebanon is well-watered and rich in forests, especially cedar, which was used for the Jerusalem temple (1 Kin. 5:6–10).
Lit. “consecrate.” Language normally used of war undertaken by God for His people is used, shockingly, of a foreign army arrayed against God’s people (6:4, 5; 21:4, 5).
Josiah and his son Shallum (v. 11). Shallum, also known as Jehoahaz, reigns briefly and is exiled to Egypt in 609 B.C. (2 Kin. 23:30–34). This saying probably dates from that year.
Expensive architectural touches paid for by oppressive taxation of the poor.

verse_quote: Do you think ... well with him.
note: The contrast is between kingship seen as the exercise of justice (Josiah) and kingship as an opportunity for getting wealth (Jehoiakim).

verse_quote: Is not this to know me.
note: See note on Ps. 9:18. Knowing the Lord requires being faithful to His commands (Mic. 6:6–8; John 14:15, 17).

Jehoiakim.

**dishonest gain ... innocent blood ... oppression.** Jehoiakim is guilty of all of the evils Jeremiah condemns (6:13; 7:6; 19:4; 21:12; and cf. 26:20–23).
The extreme shame of no burial, rather than the kind of burial given to family members or respected leaders. See 7:33; 8:1, 2 and notes; cf. 15:3.

These mountainous regions lie to the north, northeast, and southeast, respectively. Jerusalem is pictured as wailing for help to former allies (her “lovers”), themselves now powerless before Babylon, leaving Jerusalem to cry alone.

verse_quote: the wind shall shepherd all your shepherds.
note: The wind often represents the Lord’s judgment (e.g., 4:11); the shepherds are Judah’s kings. See note on 2:8.

In the present context, this phrase is a figure for Jerusalem. (The phrase itself is related to the close trade connections between Jerusalem and Lebanon.) The temple and palace were built with cedar from Lebanon (v. 6 note). The name connotes Judah’s pride and false sense of security.

Oracle against Jehoiachin (here called “Coniah”), after whose brief reign (December 598–March 597 B.C.) the first major deportations to Babylon occur.
