**22:24 signet.** Represents the identity of the owner and is used to sign important documents. To reject it is shocking. This indicates a temporary end to the promise to David and his line. Jehoiachin is the last in the direct line of Davidic kings. Zedekiah, who succeeded him and who reigns when the Babylonians destroy Jerusalem, was Jehoicahin’s uncle. Later, the same language is used to promise a renewal of the Davidic kingdom (Hag. 2:23).
See note on 21:4.

verse_quote: I will hurl you and the mother who bore you.
note:
See 13:18 and note. For other instances of “hurl,” see 1 Sam. 18:11; Jon. 1:4.

**into another country.** This reference to exile in Babylon is fulfilled in 597 B.C. (29:2; 2 Kin. 24:15).
Jehoiachin is like the shattered clay vessel of ch. 19.

In this address to the land, the Lord expresses His grief over His inheritance that has been defiled by Judah’s sin (2:7 and note; 12:4). The triple repetition adds emphasis, as with the triple repetition of “holy” in Is. 6.

verse_quote: Write this man down as childless.
note: Though Jehoiachin had seven sons (1 Chr. 3:17, 18), none of them will reign as king over Judah. Promises of future Davidic kingship (e.g., 23:5, 6) are fulfilled beyond the scope of the historical Israelite and Judahite kingdoms—in Christ the Son of Man (Dan. 7:13 and note) and the greatest son of David (Matt. 22:41–46). Even the promise to Zerubbabel (Hag. 2:23), Jehoiachin’s grandson (1 Chr. 3:19), finds fulfillment in Christ, since Zerubbabel never reigns as king. After Zerubbabel, the monarchy is essentially abandoned until the coming of Christ (Mic. 5:3).

The kings of Judah. It is typical of the prophets to use language imbued with shepherd imagery in order to criticize royalty. Elsewhere, shepherd imagery is used positively to speak of exemplary leadership (cf. Ps. 23).

The failure of the kings requires the Lord Himself to take control in a new way (24:7 note).

**remnant.** The gathering of the remnant shows the continuing care of the Lord for His people and His determination to fulfill His covenantal purposes. In the present context, the doctrine of the remnant suggests first of all the breaking off of certain of Judah’s branches (vv. 1, 2; cf. Rom. 11:17–24) following the king’s neglect and the due punishment (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes).

**bring them back to their fold.** The Lord Himself is now the Shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34:11), a role that Jesus takes up in the NT (John 10:14).

verse_quote: I will set shepherds over them.
note: Under the Shepherd there will be true shepherds who will faithfully administer the kingdom in the new age (Mic. 5:5; 1 Pet. 5:2–4).

This messianic promise is a fulfillment of the promise to David (2 Sam. 7:12; Matt. 1:1, 17) and follows repeated indictments against Judah’s shepherd leaders. Despite the coming judgment, the Lord will install a future Davidic king.

**23:5 a righteous Branch.** A messianic term. See Is. 4:2; 11:1; and Zech. 6:12, where Zerubbabel is a type of Christ.

**execute justice and righteousness.** See note on 21:12. This messianic King will be quite unlike Zedekiah and Jehoiakim.

**23:6 Judah ... Israel.** The reunification of Judah and Israel marks the messianic age (Ezek. 37:15–22).

**securely.** The blessings of the messianic kingdom will include deliverance from the political and military turmoil surrounding Judah. The Sinai covenant promises this as the reward for obedience, but old covenant Israel never experiences it because of her repeated disobedience. In the future, the Messiah’s own righteous obedience will usher in this long-awaited peace for His people.

**name.** In Scripture, names are understood as designations of character, not arbitrary labels. See “Immanuel” in Is. 7:14 and the names in Is. 9:6.

**The LORD is our righteousness.** Righteous rule is the hallmark of the Messiah’s reign. Zedekiah’s name means “the Lord is righteous.”

verse_quote: out of the land of Egypt.
note: Until this point in old covenant history, the exodus from Egypt has been the paradigm of deliverance. This future salvation from the north country (Babylon) will so far exceed the Egyptian experience as to replace it as the new paradigm of redemption.

See theological note “The Prophets of God” on p. 279.

**like a drunken man.** Judgment is frequently compared to drunkenness in the OT (Is. 51:21–23; Jer. 25:15, 16): a state of staggering and confusion that ends with falling down and being unable to get up. As a prophet, Jeremiah identifies with those against whom he is prophesying and feels within himself the judgment that is coming upon them. The false prophets have no such compassion or empathy.

These groups are supposed to communicate the Lord’s will to the people through bringing the word and teaching the law. If these men are ungodly, how can God’s people be expected to find the way of truth?

Right belief and right action are inseparable in the OT; it is no accident that those who have not heard God’s revelation actively encourage evil. See 29:21–23. This may refer to spiritual adultery as well as to physical adultery. The prophets of the southern kingdom of Judah have become just like the prophets of the old northern kingdom of Israel, which has long since been destroyed by God’s judgment.

**like Sodom ... like Gomorrah.** See 20:16; Is. 1:9 and notes. The comparison of Jerusalem to Sodom and Gomorrah is shocking and ominous.
See Jer. 9:15. The imagery in these verses describes a shocking reversal. Instead of a rich banquet, the Lord serves a meal of bitterness and poison.

verse_quote: stood in the council of the
note: LORD**.** The Hebrew word translated “council” here and in v. 22 may also be translated “counsel,” depending on whether the emphasis is on God’s deliberations with the heavenly “council” (1 Kin. 22:19–22; Job 1:6) or on the “counsel” resulting from those deliberations. The word is translated “secret” in Amos 3:7.
LORD**.** Entering the presence of the Lord is often likened to experiencing a storm or a tempest (see Job 38:1; Ezek. 1:4).
This does not refer to the end times, but rather to the fact that subsequent events will show the truth of a prophet’s words. Jeremiah’s prophecies are later vindicated by the fall of Jerusalem.

See 14:14.

**yet they ran ... prophesied.** The prophets are a picture of zeal in their self-serving propagation of falsehood. See theological note “Prophets” on p. 279.
See note on v. 18.
Nothing, near or far, can escape God’s knowledge (Ps. 139:2; Amos 9:2, 3). The Lord is not tied to a particular geographical location, as the pagan gods are.
See theological note “The Omnipresence of God” on previous page.

The dream is one way in which a revelation might come to a prophet (Num. 12:6; cf. Joel 2:28); yet such claims should always be treated with due suspicion and tested against the rest of God’s revelation (Deut. 13:1–3).
The false dream is to the true prophetic word as straw is to wheat; only the wheat has any value. The question “What has straw in common with wheat?” probably reflects a contemporary proverb.
There can be no mistaking the true word because of its inevitable effects (Amos 3:8).
For a case of prophetic jealousy, see 1 Kin. 22:24.

verse_quote: declares the LORD ... and declare, ‘declares the
note: LORD**.’** The false prophets disguise their own words as words from God by using the prophetic formula. Alternatively, the Septuagint, instead of “and declare, ‘declares the Lord,’” has “and sleep their sleep,” which comes from a different but related Hebrew root.

This word is typically used in judgment oracles. The people’s desire for a message from God might sound spiritual, but it is actually a rebellious refusal to listen to the clear word that He has already declared to them.

A vision of two baskets of figs, one representing those exiled to Babylon and the other those who will resist exile and with it the Lord’s purpose of judgment and salvation. This prophecy reveals that it is too late to avert the exile by repentance (21:9).

**24:1 Jeconiah ... to Babylon.** The first large deportation was in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:14–16). Jeconiah is yet another name for Jehoiachin, who is also known as Coniah (22:24).

**placed before the temple.** Represent an offering of the firstfruits: the good figs are accepted while the bad figs are rejected.

verse_quote: very good figs ... very bad figs.
note: Those who remain behind in Judah regard the people sent into exile as self-evidently under God’s judgment. However, this vision reveals that the exiles are the remnant that will be preserved for God’s purposes (“good figs”), while those who remain in Judah are beyond redemption and can only be destroyed by judgment (“bad figs,” vv. 8–10).
See note on 21:4.

The Lord’s plan for the exiles is positive: to build them up and plant them, not to tear them down or uproot them (cf. 1:10). The vocabulary of this section displays many similarities to the account of Jeremiah’s call in 1:4–19.

verse_quote: I will give them a heart to know.
note:
The Lord’s answer to His people’s inability to maintain the covenant relationship is that He Himself will intervene and create in them a new capacity for knowing Him.

**they shall be my people and I will be their God.** Use of the basic covenant formula (32:38; Lev. 26:12) shows that this answer is nothing less than a new covenant. The theology introduced here is developed at 31:31–34.

verse_quote: those who dwell in the land of Egypt.
note: Some people flee to Egypt before, during, and after the Babylonian invasion (see ch. 43). Yet even though these people have escaped the judgment of God on the earthly plane, they are not included in the good figs. The future of the Lord’s people lies with those undergoing the exile in Babylon.

Jeremiah predicts seventy years of Babylonian captivity for Judah as judgment for persistent sin, and he warns the neighboring nations as well of judgment at the hands of Babylon (ch. 25). His message meets opposition from false prophets, priests, and the people (chs. 26–29).

**25:1 fourth year of Jehoiakim.** The Babylonian armies move down the Mediterranean coast in 605 B.C., and Judah becomes a vassal state. This is the same year in which Jeremiah dictates a message of judgment that his scribe, Baruch, reads to King Jehoiakim (ch. 36).

See 1:2 and notes.

**persistently.** Jeremiah’s persistence is part of a long prophetic mission to Israel. He has been preaching for twenty-three years at the time this oracle is given. The faithful prophets Uriah (26:20–23), Zephaniah, and Habakkuk are also prophesying during this time. Like his predecessors and contemporaries, Jeremiah does not receive a positive response to his ministry (7:13 and note).

verse_quote: Turn now, every one of you.
note: An apt summary of what all of the faithful prophets of the Lord said to the people. Jeremiah’s message to the old covenant community is that obedience to the Mosaic covenant is essential if the people are to stay in the land God has given them.

Babylon and her allies (1:15; 6:1).

Is. 41:8–14; 43:1–5., 28

The Egyptians attacked Israel’s old enemy the Philistines on several occasions, including an assault before the Battle of Megiddo in 609 B.C. and also in 601 B.C. Yet the Philistines’ downfall will not come at the hands of the Egyptians but rather the Babylonians, the “waters ... rising out of the north” (1:13, 14 note)., 2

These Phoenician cities afford natural protection to the Philistines farther down the Mediterranean coast, though it is not known whether alliances ever exist between them.

**Caphtor.** The Philistines’ place of origin, usually identified as Crete.
Ritual mourning practices for pagans include cutting themselves and shaving their heads.
LORD**.** This instrument of the Lord’s judgment is unsheathed against His own people in Ezek. 21:9–17. Now it will come on their neighbors.

This chapter records the oracle against Moab; cf. Is. 15; 16; Ezek. 25:8–11; Amos 2:1–3. Moab was Israel’s enemy (Judg. 3:12–14; 2 Kin. 3:4–27). It was an ally of Judah against Babylon (27:3), but supplied troops for Nebuchadnezzar against Jehoiakim (2 Kin. 24:2). Its defeat by Nebuchadnezzar may have come in 582 B.C. after a rebellion.

**48:1 Nebo ... Kiriathaim.** Originally these towns were allocated to the tribe of Reuben (Num. 32:3, 37, 38; Josh. 13:15, 19). Since they are in the northern part of Moab, they will be overrun first in a Babylonian invasion.

A village northeast of Mount Nebo; it was also assigned to Reuben (Num. 32:37; Josh. 13:17).

**48:2** –**5 Madmen ... Horonaim ... Luhith.** A similar reference to Luhith and Horonaim occurs in Is. 15:5. Horonaim also appears on the Moabite Stone, from the ninth century B.C. The name “Madmen” is a play on words: it sounds like the Hebrew word for “silence.”
Junipers are hardy evergreen trees that cling to life in hostile environments.
A god of Moab worshiped by Solomon (1 Kin. 11:7, 33; 2 Kin. 23:13). Images of defeated gods were often carried off into exile.
Probably Nebuchadnezzar.

The wine left to age represents Moab’s complacency. Moab has been left untouched while the surrounding nations are invaded. Its ease and security will vanish as quickly as a bottle empties when overturned., 12

Possibly a reference to the name “El Bethel” used for the Lord in Jeroboam’s apostate worship at Bethel (1 Kin. 12:28–30). That cult did not prevent the Assyrians from plundering the land in 722 B.C. (2 Kin. 18:9–12).
Like Egypt, Moab puts its confidence in the power of its soldiers (see 46:3–6). Its trust will be equally misplaced.

verse_quote: How the mighty scepter is broken.
note: A lament for Moab (cf. 2 Sam. 1:19). The prophets sing laments for those who are not yet dead as a sign of the certainty of their coming downfall (cf. Ezek. 19). The scepter and the staff are symbols of Moab’s power, now broken.
Southeast of Dibon, this border fortress on the Arnon River (v. 20) is here pictured anxiously watching the flight of the refugees.
The region along the Arnon. It is the most important river in Moab in Jeremiah’s day.
Drunkenness is a symbol of Judah’s judgment (see 25:15–29); now it is Moab’s turn to be judged.
Moab mocked Judah for her fate, asserting that she deserved to be destroyed for her sins. Although that was true, Moab was no better and in no position to look down on Judah.
See Is. 2:10.

See Is. 16:8. This area at the northern end of the Dead Sea is famous for its orchards and vineyards. The joyful shouts of those treading the grapes will be replaced by shouts of anguish and pain (see 25:30)., 33
These local places of pagan worship will be eliminated from Moab, just as they have been destroyed in Judah (see 17:3).
The music of the flute often accompanies ceremonies both joyful and sad.
Signs of mourning. See note on 41:5.
It is customary in Jeremiah’s day to offer incense upon rooftops as an act of worship (2 Kin. 23:12).
Nebuchadnezzar (Ezek. 17:3).

Derived from Num. 21:28, 29, but Jeremiah redirects Balaam’s prophecy against the Amorites by applying it to Moab.

**48:45 Sihon.** An Amorite ruler in Moses’s time, with his capital at Heshbon (Num. 21:21–30).
Like Egypt (see 46:26), even Moab can repent and be added to the Lord’s people.

A prophecy against the Ammonites. See Ezek. 25:1–7; Amos 1:13–15. Ammon, an old enemy of Israel (Judg. 11:4–33; 1 Sam. 11:1–11; 2 Sam. 10; 1 Kin. 4:13–19), is located in Transjordan just north of Moab. Like Moab, it was part of an alliance against Babylon (27:3), and like Moab it supplied troops to Nebuchadnezzar against Judah (2 Kin. 24:2). Its hostility to Gedaliah (40:13–41:3) suggests a rebellion against Babylon, probably leading to an attack that virtually ends its existence as an autonomous nation.

**49:1 Milcom.** Chief god of the Ammonites, also known as Molech (32:35 note; 1 Kin. 11:5).

**Gad.** This Israelite tribe settled in the Transjordan before the conquest of the Promised Land proper (Num. 32). The Ammonites took it from them more than a century before the time of Jeremiah, claiming that it belonged to their god, Molech.
This city is identified with modern Amman in Jordan. It is the capital of the Ammon­ites; once it is reduced to ruins, the Israelites will reclaim their inheritance.

As a border town, it may have belonged to Ammon at some time also (Judg. 11:26).

**Ai.** Not the city of Ai familiar from the events of Josh. 8. Its location is unknown.

**Milcom shall go into exile** . See note on 48:7. The Lord is judging Moab’s gods as well as Moab itself.

verse_quote: terror ... from all who are around you.
note: Reminiscent of the phrase “terror on every side” (see 6:25; 20:3; 46:5).
See note on 48:27. This message should encourage the Lord’s people in exile as well. If Egypt, Moab, and Ammon can be restored, how much more the Lord’s own people?

A prophecy against Edom. See also 27:3; cf. Is. 21:11, 12; Ezek. 25:12–14; Amos 1:11, 12; Obad. 1–16. Edom, the descendants of Jacob’s estranged brother Esau, is an old enemy of Israel (2 Sam. 8:13, 14) and has caused special bitterness by assisting Babylon against Judah.

**49:7, 8 Teman ... Dedan.** These regions represent the northern and southern limits of Edom (see Ezek. 25:13).

**49:8 Esau.** Jacob’s brother, whose name is another designation for Edom (Gen. 25:29, 30). See Obad. 10.
Cf. Obad. 5. Both of these groups tend to leave something behind no matter how careful they are. Yet when the Babylonians come, there will be nothing left.

verse_quote: those who did not deserve to drink the cup.
note: The image of bitter wine for the judgment of God is common in the Prophets (see 25:15–17; 34:5, 6). “Those who did not deserve to drink the cup” may be a reference to faithful Judeans who, like Baruch and Jeremiah, have been caught up in the destruction of their homeland nonetheless.
The capital of Edom.
The Edomites are confident that the inaccessibility of their cities will protect them. Yet no natural advantages can protect a city from the wrath of the Lord.

In Jeremiah’s day, lions roam the lush terrain of the Jordan valley and threaten shepherds (1 Sam. 17:37). In 4:7, the roaring lion was Nebuchadnezzar. Here it is the Lord, the One whose wrath stands behind Nebuchadnezzar.
Probably Nebuchadnezzar (as 48:40), though the Edomites are also conquered decisively by Arabs during the sixth century B.C.

A prophecy against the city-states of Syria (Aram), of which Damascus is the most significant. Syria impinges chiefly on the northern kingdom of Israel in the Assyrian period (1 Kin. 20; Amos 1:3–5). The three states named here fell to Assyria in the eighth century B.C.

**49:23 Damascus ... Hamath ... Arpad.** Major Aramean city-states. Hamath and Arpad are both north of Damascus and will therefore be the first to be affected by a Babylonian invasion.
This is not a personal name but rather a dynastic title that identifies the ruler of Syria as the son of the god Hadad.

A prophecy against Arabian kingdoms. Arab nomadic tribes pose a periodic threat to settled communities in the ancient world (Judg. 6:1–6). The present prophecy may be occasioned by an Arab uprising against Nebuchadnezzar in 598 B.C. They have few cities, so the judgment is aimed at the markers of wealth in their community—tents, flocks, and camels.

**49:28 Kedar.** An Arab tribe well known in the OT period (Gen. 25:13; Is. 21:16, 17; 42:11).

**Hazor.** Also in the Arabian desert, and not the well-known Hazor in northern Israel. This name may designate a number of Arab settlements, including Teman, Buz, and Dedan (25:23, 24).

**people of the east.** Another designation for Arab tribal peoples (Judg. 6:3; 7:12; Job 1:3).

verse_quote: dwells securely ... no gates or bars.
note: These nomadic peoples typically live in unwalled towns, not depending on fortified cities. See the description of Laish in Judg. 18:7. They are no match for a well-armed invader.
Animals known to haunt desolate ruins (see Mal. 1:3).

A prophecy against Elam, an important power to the east of Babylon, subjugated by Assyria but resurgent in the Babylonian period. The prophecy possibly relates to a Babylonian containment campaign against Elam in 595 B.C. Unlike the other prophecies in this section, the oracle against Elam is dated to the beginning of Zedekiah’s reign in 597 B.C. At that time, some in Judah may have hoped that a resurgent Elam would neutralize the Babylonian threat and result in the swift return of those already exiled.
Elam is famous for its archers.

verse_quote: I will set my throne in Elam.
note: Nebuchadnezzar’s destruction of Elam has nothing to do with the gods of the Babylonians. It is a sign of the Lord’s sovereign rule over all nations.

The prophecy against Babylon (cf. Is. 13:1–14:23; 21:1–9) is the climax of the book. The previous prophecies have served Jeremiah’s purpose of showing that Babylon will prevail over “all the nations” for a period (27:7). Babylon has appeared up to this point as the instrument of God’s wrath. Finally, however (as in 25:17–26), “the word that the Lord spoke” is uttered against Bab­ylon itself to show that its own time of judgment must come (25:11, 12). The Hebrew text of Jeremiah has placed the prophecy (actually delivered in 593 B.C.; cf. 51:59 note) at this point in the book so that the judgment on Babylon can occupy the climactic position. The relative length of the prophecy also shows how important Babylon is in the theology of the book.

Merodach, or “Marduk,” is the creator and chief deity in Babylonian myth. He is also called Bel, an early form of the word “Baal” (“lord”). See also Is. 46:1. He is nothing more than a powerless idol, however.

verse_quote: out of the north a nation.
note: See 1:14; 6:1. Normally in the book of Jeremiah, the enemy from the north country is Babylon. The tables are now turned on Babylon. The nation in question is not specified, but see 51:27, 28, where it is clear that the reference is to the Medes and the Persians.

verse_quote: people of Israel and the people of Judah.
note:
The report of Babylon’s impending downfall is good news for God’s own people, who will then be able to return to worship the Lord at Zion, the site of the temple in Jerusalem.

**50:5 everlasting covenant.** See 31:31–34; 32:40; 33:20, 21. Unlike the previous covenant, which the people broke, this one will never be forgotten.

verse_quote: Their shepherds have led them astray.

note: This claim on the part of the enemies of God’s people is refuted by the surrounding oracle of judgment against Babylon. God will hold those who assault His people to account even though He has brought these nations in judgment against them.

verse_quote: Flee from the midst of Babylon.
note: When the day of Babylon’s judgment comes, it will be time for God’s people to return home to Judah. See Is. 48:20; Zech. 2:6. The edict issued by Cyrus in 539 B.C., shortly after Babylon’s destruction, allows the Jews and other captured peoples to go home.

verse_quote: I am stirring up ... against Babylon . . . from the north country.
note: Cyrus is mentioned as the leader of this alliance of the Medes and Persians in Is. 41:25; 45:1. Members of the alliance are named in 51:27, 28.
The Lord’s continuing concern for His promises to His people is clear. Those who assault Israel will pay the price (see Gen. 12:3).

Babylon is personified.

**last of the nations.** She who has seemed invincible will be completely devastated (Is. 14:12–17).
The references to the kings of Assyria and Babylon make it clear that “Israel” here is not the former northern kingdom but the original people of God, made up of all twelve tribes.

verse_quote: Carmel ... Bashan ... hills of Ephraim and in Gilead.
note: The most fertile parts of Israel, famous for their livestock (see Amos 4:1).
The Lord promises to do something in the future that will remove completely the sins of His people. Cf. Zech. 3:9.
These words are puns on Babylonian place-names (Marratu, Puqudu). The Hebrew words mean “double rebellion” and “punishment.”
Hammers are used for breaking up rocks (23:19). Here the hammer itself will be shattered.

verse_quote: taken ... you did not know it.
note: The Persian defeat of Babylon is unexpected.
Babylon’s army (46:15 note).

Jewish escapees from Babylon will return to Jerusalem, where they will testify to the Lord’s deliverance.

**vengeance for his temple.** The burning of the temple (52:13) was the definitive destruction of Jerusalem. The Lord ties His vengeance on Babylon specifically to that.

Unlike in the fall of Judah, there will be no remnant surviving the fall of Babylon.

**the Holy One of Israel.** This name for God is frequent in Isaiah (cf. Is. 1:4 note). No one can defy the true and living God and escape the consequences.

–**38 The people of Israel are oppressed ... they refuse to let them go.** The background for these verses is the exodus, when God brought Israel out of captivity in Egypt. Similar language is now applied to the oppressive Babylon. A new exodus will ensue in which God will subdue the Babylonians and deliver His people once more.
See note on 31:11. When the Lord steps in as their advocate, the result is rest for His people and unrest for her tormentors.

–**40 the Chaldeans.** See note on 21:4. Everything in which the Babylonians might trust—wise men, diviners, warriors, horses and chariots, mercenaries, treasures, the waters that surround the city—will prove to be unworthy of such trust. The ruins will be abandoned to wild animals such as hyenas and ostriches (or possibly “screech owls”; the exact identity of the bird is not clear). Its downfall will be as complete and permanent as that of Sodom and Gomorrah.

verse_quote: a people comes from the north.
note: Compare the almost identical description of the Babylonian armies coming against Judah in 6:22–24. Now they will be invaded by such an oppressor.
Cf. 49:19–22, where Babylon’s assault of Edom is described in similar terms.

A coded reference to “Kasdim” or the Chaldeans (text note), another name for Babylon. It uses the same code as the name “Sheshach” in 25:26 and 51:41 (text notes), in which the last letter of the alphabet is substituted for the first, the second last for the second, and so on.
Babylon is to be treated according to the rules of holy war. No one is to be spared alive and no plunder is to be taken, for everything belongs to the Lord.

verse_quote: Flee from the midst of Babylon.
note: See note on 50:8.
Babylon has been the agent of the Lord’s destruction of many nations (25:15). Now she herself will have to drink from that bitter cup.
The sudden destruction of this seemingly invincible city is a symbol of the end for all of God’s enemies. See Rev. 18:2.
Babylon is finally conquered by an alliance of Medes and Persians, including Darius the Mede (see Dan. 6; Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). See also Is. 13:17; 21:2.
Babylon is renowned for its irrigation channels, fed by the Euphrates River. In the same way, the great prostitute of Rev. 17:1 sits on many waters.
See Gen. 22:16 and note.

–**19** The Lord’s power and wisdom, which are evident in His work of creation, will be harnessed to the task of Babylon’s destruction with equally impressive results. Cf. 10:12–16. In comparison to Him, the idols of the nations are worthless and powerless. They will be destroyed along with all those who trust in them.

Apparently addressed to Babylon, vv. 20–23 should be taken together with vv. 24–26. Babylon has been God’s “hammer” (50:23) against the nations, but Bab­ylon’s own sin will later cause it to be judged.

In Dan. 2:35, a small stone becomes a mountain that fills the entire earth. Here Babylon begins as an enormous mountain that destroys much of the earth but then shrinks into a rock that can be rolled off a cliff and then burned. No foundation stone or cornerstone will come from it (cf. Is. 28:16)., 26
Districts of Media that are now summoned to join the fight against Babylon.
Babylon’s sacking of Judah (cf. 21:10) is being avenged by her Median conquerors.

verse_quote: the marshes are burned with fire.
note: A possible route of escape from the city of Babylon is blocked.

This figure both personifies Babylon and alludes to its women, made vulnerable by defeat. See 50:42; Lam. 1:6 and note.

**a threshing floor.** An area that has been trodden hard and flat, where the harvested wheat is taken to be beaten with sticks to separate the grain from the chaff.

Hb. _tannin._ Used to describe the great sea creatures in Gen. 1:21 and the multi-headed sea monster Leviathan in Ps. 74:13. It is often an image of something far more terrifying than a normal creature.
See 50:15. The metaphors of revenge and courtroom judgment are mixed here.
See note on 9:11.
The Hebrew has “Sheshach” here (text note); cf. notes on 25:26; 51:1.

See note on 50:2. Instead of the nations flowing to Bel, in the last days they will flow to Zion, to the Lord (see Is. 2:2).

**what he has swallowed.** Bel has “swallowed” the nations taken into exile and their treasures (see v. 34). Judah’s treasures are later restored by Cyrus’s decree (Ezra 1:5–11).

**wall of Babylon.** An enormously wide double wall, further protected by an intervening moat.

verse_quote: Go out of the midst of her.
note: God’s people should be prepared for the coming day when they will leave their exile and return home. Though it is still many years distant and there will be conflicting reports at the time,they should maintain a constant state of readiness for the Lord’s day of judgment on Babylon, which would be their own day of deliverance.

The exiles express their grief over the occupation of the temple by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C., perhaps feeling that this defilement can never be cleansed. Yet they must continue to remember Jerusalem even though they are far away in exile. Cf. Ps. 137., 51

verse_quote: Though Babylon should mount up to heaven.
note: Probably a reference to its lofty ziggurats, symbols of its religious pride (Gen. 11:4).

verse_quote: the LORD is a God of recompense.
note: Unlike the idols, which can say and do nothing, the Lord acts to defend His people and judge their enemies (see vv. 35, 36).

The Ishtar Gate is known for its great height.

**labor ... the nations.** The labor of subject nations in building Babylon’s fortifications will be of no use when God brings His judgment.

An official in Zedekiah’s administration, he is responsible for this expedition’s lodging en route. He is the brother of Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe (32:12).

**went with Zedekiah ... to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign.** 593 B.C. The expedition may be in response to a summons to explain Zedekiah’s part in the uprising against Nebuchadnezzar (27:3 note). Jeremiah knows the ultimate destiny of Babylon even as he urges his countrymen to submit to Nebuchadnezzar (38:1–3).
It may contain the prophecies in chs. 50 and 51. See 36:2.
This final symbolic act (13:1–11 note) reinforces the last word of Jeremiah that Babylon will fall as completely and comprehensively as a scroll tied to a stone and cast into the Euphrates., 64

The final chapter of Jeremiah is an appendix, largely drawn from 2 Kin. 24; 25, describing the fall of Jerusalem and reminding the reader that Jeremiah’s prophecies have been fulfilled. Despite its message of divine judgment for sin, the book of Jeremiah ends (as does 2 Kings) on a hopeful note by calling attention to the mercy shown to King Jehoiachin of Judah while in Babylonian exile (52:31–34; cf. 2 Kin. 25:27–30). The section of 2 Kings dealing with Gedaliah’s assassination is omitted here because it was dealt with in chs. 40; 41.

**52:1 Jeremiah of Libnah.** Not Jeremiah the prophet, who is from Anathoth (1:1).

verse_quote: he did what was evil in the sight of the
note: LORD**.** In the book of Kings, all of the kings of Israel and Judah are evaluated for their faithfulness in pursuing the pure worship of the people, centralized in the temple in Jerusalem. Zedekiah is judged a failure on this account.
The fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple are also described in Jer. 39:1–10.
2 Kin. 25:8 has the “seventh day.” One or the other text could be a copyist’s minor error. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

These are added to the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar has already taken from Jerusalem (see 27:16). They are returned to Jerusalem in the time of Cyrus (Ezra 1:7), providing a line of continuity between the first and second temples.
2 Kin. 25:17 has “three.” See note on v. 12.
2 Kin. 25:19 has “five.” See note on v. 12.

These verses refer to the two main deportations of Jews to Babylon in 597 B.C. (“the seventh year”) and 586 B.C. (the “eighteenth year”; “nineteenth” in v. 12 is due to an alternate way of counting). A third, smaller deportation is also mentioned, perhaps in response to the assassination of Gedaliah. The numbers here are smaller than those in 2 Kin. 24:14, 16, and may count only adult males or only the leading figures of Judah.

–**34 twenty-fifth.**2 Kin. 25:27 has “twenty-seventh.” See note on v. 12.

**52:31 Jehoiachin.** The kind treatment of the former king of Judah by Evil-Merodach (also known as Amel-Marduk) on his accession to the throne in 562 B.C. provides a glimmer of hope for the restoration of God’s people that Jeremiah prophesied. The absence of any reference to the decree of Cyrus permitting the people to return home in 539 B.C. suggests that the book of Jeremiah reached its final form before that date.
